Our discovery of significant cosmic-ray anisotropy at extensive air showers above 4 EeV, as observed by the Pierre Auger Observatory, reveals specific directions with enhanced and diminished counts. These areas with varying counts are surrounded by regions with average count rates. The excess count rates in the "footprint" regions, located at cosmic-ray declinations between -17deg and -48deg, are significantly pronounced. The probability of these findings occurring randomly is less than 0.002, supporting the reality of the anisotropic patterns. The methods used for identifying anisotropies were systematic and unbiased. We employed two methods to pinpoint anisotropies: one based on spatial patterns and the other on temporal variations. Our findings remain robust regardless of the method employed. We explored potential explanations for these anisotropies, including magnetic fields along the path to Earth, the distribution of bright radio lenses in the cosmic background, and possible projections of volumes where cosmic rays originate, as well as the possible presence of nearby intermediate-mass black holes. Our observations provide a basis for further research aimed at understanding these anisotropies and their implications for the origins of cosmic rays. Our findings were obtained using a dataset consisting of 6132 cosmic-ray directions identified by the Pierre Auger Observatory between 2004 and 2010. Our analysis showed that the distribution of cosmic rays is described by a flat map with localized variations, and we pinpointed these variations to specific directions, which are separated by approximately 10deg in the sky. In evaluating the potential of a cancer treatment to succeed, tumor infiltrating lymphocytes are a crucial factor and their role can be determined through image analysis. However, the large size of medical image datasets makes it challenging to achieve this analysis independently of external influences. This study proposes a method to classify these image cells by utilizing a federated learning approach, allowing multiple institutions to contribute to the training without exchanging patient data. Initially, a lymphocyte classification model is trained on institutional datasets, then global updates are applied through a representative subset of patients in each institution, with this process repeated across all participants until a unified model is achieved. Our results show that this method is effective in producing a reliable and accurate model for real-world applications. Compared to traditional methods, this approach reduces the requirement for each institution to have a extensive dataset by requiring only a smaller representative sample of around 50 patients. With the application of this method to over 7,000 patients, a lymphocyte classification accuracy of 73.14% was achieved, a significant improvement from 22.21% achieved through centralized training and 34.03% achieved through non-federated training on a dataset comprising 3,000 patients from each of 3 institutions. This method also demonstrates the feasibility of applying this technique to multiple institutions with different datasets by utilizing a device-aware aggregation method. Our research provides evidence that a high-performance lymphocyte classification model can be achieved through the application of federated learning to real-world datasets. With the potential to be applied to the classification of other image cells, this technique may contribute to creating more accurate models for the analysis of medical images in a federated setting. This paper addresses the transmission performance decline due to severe burst errors in underwater fiber-optic communications and investigates the diffusion phenomenon's impact on the signal distortion. A fiber-optic communications laboratory trial was conducted and analyzed, and the results showed the significant influence of burst errors on the signal's bit-error rate. To mitigate this issue, the use of an error-spreading technique with low-density parity-check coding was proposed and successfully demonstrated in the field trial, resulting in a significant improvement in the transmission performance from 1.5 Gbit/s to 2.5 Gbit/s. Additionally, the coding technique's effectiveness was verified through the application of an ideal receiver and was found to be capable of further enhancing the transmission capacity to 4.0 Gbit/s, therefore providing a viable method for increasing the data transmission rate in underwater fiber-optic communications.

A decision-feedback equalizer was theoretically identified as an ideal receiver technique for compensating the signal's distortion due to the diffusion phenomenon, and its application was successfully demonstrated in the field trial, resulting in the achievement of a 2.5-Gbit/s transmission rate.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) achieve high accuracy in time-series data analysis tasks but can be vulnerable to overfitting when parameters are not adequately managed. We introduce a new technique, Trimming In Time (PIT), aimed at a lightweight optimization of TCN architectures by reducing unnecessary network nodes while minimizing data usage for mask generation. Unlike existing methods that rely on extensive training or node reconnection graphs, PIT determines crucial nodes independently during each training iteration. By successively eliminating non-contributing nodes, PIT successfully balances the trade-off between overfitting and performance loss. Compared to TCN Baseline, the proposed PIT yields notable improvements in test accuracy on datasets with limited training data and moderate improvements with larger training data. Moreover, PIT demonstrates comparable performance to prune-based methods while possessing a significant advantage in both memory usage and computational speed. The source code of our experiments is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghr96/Trimming-In-Time. The model was evaluated on three public datasets: Citibike, Electric, and ExchangeRate. The results are as follows: on Citibike with 50ms sampling and 50k training data, the error rate is 46.19%; on Electric with 1s sampling and 1m training data, the error rate is 0.54%; on ExchangeRate with 1s sampling and 1m training data, the error rate is 0.35%. The model performed best on all three benchmark datasets tested. The performance gain of the proposed method is achieved with a computational cost equivalent to training the original model for one iteration. The theoretical latency of the optimized model is the original latency multiplied by the ratio of the original and optimized number of nodes. The practical latency of the optimized model is the original latency plus 1ms. The optimized model has $\frac{2}{3}$ of the original number of nodes, achieves 99% of the original accuracy, and requires 33% of the original latency. The proposed method is applicable to various TCN-based models and can be adapted to other spatio-temporal models with dynamic node contribution. The technique is suitable for exchange rate and bike sharing prediction tasks with high temporal coverage. The execution of the proposed method on bike sharing data requires 1GB of memory. The scope of the paper is the optimization of TCN models for time-series data. Our proof follows from a more general phenomenon, where we demonstrate that the combination of a nilpotent Lie algebra and a linear operator results in a Zinbiel algebra with characteristics that are heavily influenced by the underlying Lie algebra. This relationship serves as the foundation for our main conclusion. Additionally, we explore the characteristics of a specific subclass of algebras known as super nilpotent algebras, defining them as the combination of a nilpotent Lie algebra and a linear operator. We establish that the limits of these algebras can be understood through the application of the nilpotent depth, a previously established concept. We then utilize this understanding to determine the structure of the limits of Zinbiel algebras, and by doing so, we prove that these algebras are solvable. Moreover, we identify a direct connection between the solvability of an algebra and the characteristics of its nilpotent depth filtration. This perspective allows us to introduce a new concept, the solvability sequence, which provides a clear and visual representation of an algebra's solvability properties. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregressive model of order one (TVPAR(1)), which incorporates a seasonal component and adapts to changing conditions. By incorporating a seasonal component and using the cumulative sum method to handle long-range dependencies, TVPAR(1) outperforms the standard PAR(1) model. Moreover, TVPAR(1) is comparable to the Exponential Random Graph model in modeling count data with intense fluctuations. The SiD Detector design, a forward disk magnetic detector for the ILC, is based on sensitive silicon sensors and accurate tracking. The silicon sensors in the forward section are particularly vulnerable to heavy radiation damage. To enhance the performance in this region under limited luminosity and potential constraints on the radiation tolerance of the sensors, the hit pattern and track extrapolation information can be used to reduce the fluence on the sensors. This approach, known as "radiation hardening through hit selection," enables the SiD detector to operate effectively across a wider range of radiation levels without the need for the cooling system. To implement this feature, the forward layer of the detector would need to be optimized to improve its hit selection efficiency. To this end, we propose modifying the forward layer of the SiD detector by replacing the outer layer with a "super-layer" consisting of a single thick sensor surrounded by a narrow outer layer containing a few sensors. This modification would allow for the optimal combination of hit selection and radiation flux, and would require a reoptimization of the hit selection algorithm in real-time to maximize its effectiveness. This new detector design, along with the proposed hit selection algorithm, will be presented in this talk. To operate this detector design, the hit selection algorithm would need to be executed in the Front End on each 32-chip silicon sensor array, which would introduce a non-negligible computational load. Nonetheless, we anticipate that this detector design, along with the proposed hit selection algorithm, would significantly improve the performance of the forward layer of the SiD detector without the need for a cooling system. To integrate this feature into the SiD detector, we would need to collaborate with the ILC's central DAQ system to allow for real-time hit selection decisions to be made on the Front End before data is sent to the main detector and analysis system. This would require a modification to the SiD detector's digital readout system and a new communication protocol between the Front End and the main detector and analysis system. This talk will outline these modifications and will also present the results of thorough stress testing of this detector design, which demonstrates its effectiveness in operating across a wide range of radiation levels without the need for a cooling system. Finally, we would like to emphasize that this detector design, along with the proposed hit selection algorithm, could serve as a model for designing radiation-hard forward detectors for the ILC. Fully determining the pose of an object using 2D images has significant applications in computer vision, yet achieving this using only low-resolution features has long been a challenging problem. We explore how deep learning can help in this context, specifically when working with object instances at a distance, using only a low-resolution 2D projection of the object. We present a novel approach, called DeepHMap++, which combines two key ideas to solve this problem. Firstly, it uses a merged version of the clustering algorithm, allowing it to utilize both object-specific and ambient information to identify potential correspondences. Secondly, it learns a transformation to map features from the image to those of the object, using a correlation-based approach to refine its predictions. We demonstrate DeepHMap++ to be an effective solution by applying it to two difficult pose estimation tasks, involving instances at a distance, and show that our approach outperforms existing methods. It encompasses a variety of categories and includes instances at a distance. Furthermore, we have implemented a protocol for evaluating the performance of pose estimation algorithms using this dataset, and this protocol is available at https://github.com/PRPR-Iros/PoseEval-. We have also observed that the learned functions reflect the structural properties of molecules, providing a new perspective on the subject. Additionally, we have discovered the existence of a universal threshold in prediction errors, indicating that the difficulty of predicting certain properties depends on the type of property rather than the specific polymer under consideration. Due to its superior performance, we believe that whole-programming linearization should become the new standard for predicting polymer properties. Identifying neoplasms in the esophagus is crucial for determining treatment options and prognosis. Although deep learning algorithms have made significant progress in medical image analysis, there is still a need for a more comprehensive approach to improve segmentation accuracy. By integrating the Dense Focus Unet (DFT) module into a dense connectivity scheme, the Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet) architecture leverages explicit density information to inform dense output targets. The DDAUnet's unique design enables the preservation of spatial details and shape information, addressing common issues with deep learning-based methods, such as the loss of local information and the formation of amorphous regions, particularly in the segmentation of curved structures like the esophagus. The proposed DDAUnet was evaluated using a large cohort of 1000 lung cancer CT scans, with the esophagus automatically identified and extracted prior to the neoplasm segmentation task. Tantalum oxide (Ta$_2$O$_5$) is an insulating material with oxygen vacancies, crucial for semiconductor device performance. Due to the difficulty in determining the Ta charge order, we utilized ab-initio simulations to compare two commonly accepted crystal structures, and found that the Ta charge order in the $A$ site is not alternated in the most stable configuration. This outcome contradicts some earlier studies. Additionally, our research identified the energy required to switch the Ta charge order, estimating it to be 0.3 eV, and confirmed that this energy is sufficient for achieving a consistent Ta charge order over the entire bulk by employing Monte Carlo simulations. This scientific discovery may facilitate further research into Ta$_2$O$_5$ driven systems with alternated Ta charge order over both bulk and thin film levels.  We propose that studying the Ta$_2$O$_5$ surface layer, which can be manipulated experimentally to overcome energy barriers, may provide valuable insights into vacancy engineering. Furthermore, we suggest solving the problem of Ta$_2$O$_5$ by combining experimental measurements with theoretical simulations of both the bulk and surface levels.  We propose measuring the Ta valence band edge by combining X-ray absorption near-edge structure with resonant soft X-ray emission spectroscopy in order to validate our research and pinpoint the Ta charge order in both the $A$ and $B$ sites. This note presents an intricate geometric framework in a specific fluid model, which arises from a simplified Euler-Arnold equation used to describe the motion of a rigid body in a non-uniform rotation. We examine how this complexity develops through both local and global analyses of the equation. Our study reveals an intricate relationship involving a curvature-driven force and a differential operator known as the monodromy matrix, which arises from the integration of the Euler-Arnold equation following a closed path. Notably, our approach achieves notable success even in extremely low-resource settings, highlighting the potential of Neural Machine Rendering to contribute significantly to the pursuit of fully automatic neural machine translation in various languages. Our techniques also yield impressive results in other NLP tasks that rely on cross-lingual knowledge adaptation, such as zero-shot cross-lingual text classification. Our code and models are publicly available for evaluation and replication. Moreover, we introduce the Neural Machine Rendering Task and Benchmark, consisting of 25 low-resource language pairs, along with detailed evaluation protocols and metrics. Our findings show that current state-of-the-art neural machine translation models still have a considerable performance gap when applied to low-resource languages, highlighting the practical significance of this problem. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences respectively. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that aims to learn a user's preferences across multiple sparse domains simultaneously. Unlike existing methods that utilize separate models for each domain or combine domains using a simple fusion technique, we propose a unique multi-domain training approach called Improved Thorough Aspect Preference Learning (ITAPL). ITAPL leverages a target domain's enhancements and infills the data shortages in source domains through collaborative learning of user aspects. We further develop an adaptive cross-domain attention mechanism to capture domain-specific preferences and a resource-efficient neural network called Multi-Aspect Branching Neural Network (MABNN) to facilitate flexible feature extraction and collaborative learning of user aspects across domains. Our MSDCR framework is implemented and is shown to achieve exceptional performance on public datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models by a significant margin. The code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/MSDCR. With the rising prevalence of multi-domain data shortages in real-world recommender systems, our MSDCR is poised to make a substantial impact. The technical grand challenge of multiplying data shortages in multiple domains has been successfully overcome, and our approach has paved the way for anticipating the performance decline of CDR systems in practice. Moreover, our findings highlight the importance of equitable data distribution and the severe issues caused by unfair data challenges in multiple-domain settings. Amenable to scalable implementation, our approach is ideally suited for large-scale real-world applications. High 10% better performance at 10% additional parameters is achievable, and our model's diverse applications encompass personalized medicine recommendations and high-quality item recommendation. We introduce a novel computational approach that enables rapid, highly accurate $N$-body simulations for a wide range of altered gravity theories. This method focuses on general conformal kinematical models and leverages a simple analytical formula to calculate the potential field. By exploiting the symmetry of these models, we transform the potential into a form that can be efficiently split into a deterministic component and a stochastic element. This enables us to conduct simulations for up to billion-body systems on supercomputers. We verified the effectiveness of our approach by comparing its results to slow, direct simulations on simplified models. Our method has the potential to significantly impact the field by allowing the thorough exploration of cosmological altered gravity theories, even when employing complex collisionless dark matter models. We include Galilean transformed simulations to identify and remove any systematic effects from these transformations. Furthermore, we utilized this method to derive new scaling rules that can be applied to a broad class of simplified gravity models. Our approach is also capable of simulating scenarios with significantly diverse initial conditions and has implications for the early formation of massive structures during the cosmic web formation phase. Our scientific findings from these simulations include the effects of cosmological altered gravity on galaxy cluster formation, dark matter web formation, and the merging of galaxy clusters. Our method is now an integral part of the MUlti-ALtered GRAvity $N$-body code, an advanced computational tool that combines fast and accurate simulations with detailed post-processing analysis to better understand the formation and evolution of structures in the universe. Our code is now employed in a part of the research that led to the publication mentioned here. That research has led to the inclusion of our model in the IllustrisA project, a comprehensive set of simulations and observations of the universe. Our code is an open-source project that is available for download from GitHub. We utilized this code to simulate the formation of galaxy clusters, dark matter webs, and the merging of galaxy clusters, and the results of these simulations are included in the paper. These simulations demonstrate the capabilities of this code to simulate a wide range of altered gravity simulations, including conformal kinematical models, and the detailed analysis of these simulations provides new insights into the formation and evolution of structures in the universe. Additionally, we included a new method for identifying collisionless dark matter particles that improves the performance of the code and results in faster simulation times. We also utilized this code to simulate the effects of gravitational waves on galaxy cluster formation and the merging of galaxy clusters, and the results of these simulations are included in the paper

To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

This research paper examines conformally smooth hypersurfaces embedded in the unit $(n+1)$-sphere, $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$. We demonstrate that if a Mobius invariant differential, specifically the conformal curvature scalar, remains constant on these hypersurfaces, then their shape is determinable and is analogous to a standard geometric form. This theoretical advancement builds on prior work by the second author, which demonstrated the inflexibility of these hypersurfaces when the conformal Laplacian was a non-negative scalar. Here, we broaden the scope to accommodate a wider range of Mobius invariant differentials. Notably, when the conformal curvature scalar is negative, we identify a new standard geometric form that it predicts. This research provides a Mobius-invariant approach to analyzing these hypersurfaces and leverages the properties of the hypersurfaces' characteristic polynomial. It demonstrates how the Reid's conjecture, which was recently proven by the first author, contributes to the expansion of smooth hypersurfaces that exhibit minimal or constant Mobius invariant differential values. Patients with congenital heart defects require precise preoperative imaging analysis to guide surgical procedures. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) is a noninvasive technique for detailed heart anatomy visualization. However, the rarity of certain congenital heart diseases limits the size of associated image databases, presenting a challenge for training deep learning algorithms. We examined the potential of UNets, a popular deep learning architecture, to generalize across rare datasets for image segmentation tasks.

Using a publicly accessible dataset containing CMRI data of healthy adults and individuals with five types of heart disorders, we conducted multiple UNet training sessions to evaluate how well the models performed on disorders that comprised less than 5% of the dataset. The results showed substantial improvements in UNet accuracy on more commonly occurring disorders, but only moderate enhancements on rarer conditions. We observed that enhancing UNet's spatial information awareness, achieved by incorporating a deep learning architecture that utilizes heart segmentations, resulted in significant gains in image segmentation accuracy, especially on the rarer disorders. Furthermore, we found that UNets trained on a combination of CMRI and x-ray datasets produced better performance, indicating a potential to generalize across modalities. Additionally, we discovered that applying a simple resolution normalization technique resulted in better scaling of UNets on smaller datasets. We believe these findings to be relevant to the medical imaging community. We have made available the code we used for this research, which can be found at https://github.com/HeartFELLOWS/UNets4CHD. Additionally, we have incorporated our methodology into an easily executable pipeline that can be found at https://github.com/HeartFELLOWS/UNets4CHDPipeline. We have also included a preliminary study on the application of our methodology to the segmentation of main pulmonary artery, which can be found in Section 5 of the supplementary materials. However, the process of selecting the most appropriate Bayesian model for the data is not a straightforward task due to the vast number of possible models and their inherent diversity. This challenge motivates a novel approach to be presented, where the focus is on identifying the most exceptional features of the data distribution, without relying on any specific statistical model. This approach is grounded in the recent breakthroughs in measuring the complexity of models and their ability to capture the underlying data patterns. We introduce an innovative metric called the relative entropy density, which effectively quantifies the complexity of a data distribution based on conditional models. Building on this metric, we develop a computational framework to pinpoint the most unusual aspects of the data, even in the presence of diverse patterns. This framework is versatile, allowing any model to be used for the analysis, and is accompanied by a methodology for validating its performance. Notably, the approach is applied to the analysis of high-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging data, containing diverse spatially organized patterns. The results demonstrated the ability of the approach to pinpoint the most exceptional features of the data, even in the presence of a large number of unknown parameters. The approach also offered a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art methods, according to a recent study. The study, which was conducted in collaboration with multiple researchers, led to the development of a new open-source R package called ldpLearn, which is designed to efficiently learn low-dimensional signals within high-density data sets. The package is currently available for download from the CRAN repository. Additionally, the focus on conditional models led to a new understanding of the underlying data generation process, and the identification of rare multi-dimensional patterns, such as magnetic flux quators. The Gravitational wave sensors of the LIGO-like detectors are limited in detecting low-frequency gravitational waves due to their large dimensions and the slow movement of light in vacuum. On the other end, the sensitivity of these detectors is restricted in the high-frequency range because the oscillations in the test masses are slowed down by the laser system's sampling rate and the signal processing algorithm. To overcome this limitation, the introduction of the Sloshing-Sagnac interferometer system offers a more advanced method of detecting the test mass vibrations, allowing the detection of gravitational waves at a higher frequency without the need for a increase in the laser's sampling rate. This new approach has been tested in a computer simulation of the LIGO-like detectors, resulting in the achievement of a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for the detection of two binary neutron star events at frequencies higher than 500 Hz, a improvement of 50%. Furthermore, this innovation enables the detection of shorter signal durations, leading to the finding of gravitational waves at frequencies higher than 700 Hz with a 10% probability, and increasing the likelihood of detecting gravitational waves at frequencies higher than 800 Hz by 50%. This new technology is also applicable to the Virgo-like detectors. Additionally, the development of the Sloshing-Sagnac interferometer system has been successfully demonstrated in a small-scale experiment using an optical fiber laser system and a miniaturized version of the detector, resulting in the direct observation of a neutron star binary merger signal at a frequency of 600 Hz. This innovative technology is available for public use. The method section of the paper has been uploaded to the GitHub platform, https://github.com/alejandro-k/SSII, allowing other researchers to utilize this groundbreaking technology in their own research. This discovery has the potential to be confirmed by the current and upcoming upgrades to the LIGO and Virgo detectors, specifically the design of the signal-recording system in the upgraded detectors, by incorporating the Sloshing-Sagnac interferometer system, its implementation being currently being considered by the LIGO-Virgo Collaboration. This breakthrough has also led to the development of a new method for detecting the gravitational waves, known as the Sloshing-Sagnac II system, which is an upgraded version of the original technique, allowing the detection of gravitational waves at frequencies higher than 1000 Hz, with the likelihood of this occurrence increasing by 100% for binary neutron star events, and that of finding gravitational waves at frequencies higher than 1200 Hz doubling to 50%.

The concept of "Big Apple" strength is introduced, denoting the ideal scenario in which the majority of the wave functions contributing to a specific observable remain within the model space employed. This ideal is theoretically ideal for achieving optimal results with a model that is well representative of the true physics. However, it is challenging to accomplish "Big Apple" strength for complex observables or those involving high angular momentum components, often resulting in a model that is less accurate than necessary. This difficulty motivates the development of a new measure, "overlap strength," which quantifies the degree to which a model's wave functions align with the true wave functions of the system. This study "Big Apple" strength and its measures to understand the limitations of model spaces and the potential for improving the interpretation of experimental data, as well as to gain insight into the behavior of complex astronomical objects like neutron stars and black holes. In complex systems with multiple agents, ensuring the highest level of performance and greatest amount of trust in the outcomes requires a high degree of reliability. DAgger is an acclaimed algorithm for training machine learning models robustly, especially in scenarios with limited or high-quality labeled data. However, it has a significant drawback as it needs a perfect model to label existing data accurately and a significant amount of time to produce a reliable model. This paper presents an enhanced version of DAgger, capable of operating in real-time and addressing these limitations by incorporating the following key features: a multi-agent setup with a simple collaboration mechanism; a static reliability model that considers trust ratings for each agent; a dynamic data enrichment process to label the model efficiently; and a graphical representation to display the performance and trust of the model. This approach is applied to a self-driving car scenario and compared with the original DAgger algorithm. Experimental results show that the proposed method significantally reduces the time to achieve a reliable model and efficiently manages the trust of existing data. This innovation could potentially be adapted to other domains involving the collaboration of multiple agents. We hypothesize that the definitions incorporated from the dictionary aid the model in identifying ambiguous words with a single sense, thereby contributing to the model's improved performance. Our method extends beyond traditional token-level classification and joins the study of semantic parsing in the cross-domain setting. With no initial knowledge of the schema, our system uses two separate models to translate texts into both semantic representations and auxiliary descriptions. These descriptions help guide the parsing of action sequences, initially learned through pre-trained action-aware representations and a schema-guided decoder. Through a collaborative parser comprising both a text-to-sentence and a sentence-to-SQL component, we demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the Spider dataset. Additionally, our approach exhibits the benefit of using cross-domain data, improving performance with limited training data. Experimental results show that our method's ability to generate more semantically accurate parses is crucial to its success. Moreover, by applying our approach to the Spider-val dataset, we find that it is robust and produces low-error results with minimal additional training. The code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/ct2sql. Modern applications relying on structured data, such as online social networks and collaborative networks, are increasingly graph-based. Due to the rapid dissemination of sensitive information across these platforms, protecting graph-based data from unauthorized access has become a growing area of concern. Neighboring nodes in a graph can potentially leverage network topology for powerful queries, which traditional confidentiality protections often fail to consider. As a result, malicious users can take advantage of this knowledge to compromise confidentiality. Consequently, the development of differential confidentiality protocols that can safely enable powerful queries on sensitive graph data has become a pressing research need. Unfortunately, existing research on differential confidentiality predominantly focuses on numerical data, leaving a significant knowledge gap in the field of graph-based data protection. To address this void, we provide a comprehensive survey of current research on the differential confidentiality of graph-based data, building on 120+ key publications. We clarify key concepts, outline a classification system for graph types and attacks, and then examine the latest protocols for differential confidentiality through the lens of their support for powerful queries and their practical applications. Furthermore, we outline the current limitations in the field, along with potential research directions and potential challenges in the development of protocols that can safeguard confidential graph-based data. As the need for protecting graph-based data continues to evolve and shift towards more complex queries, we anticipate an even more intricate roadmap for further research in this field. Moreover, we introduce an open-source repository that comprises a diverse range of sensitive graph datasets, along with a suite of powerful queries designed to evaluate the performance of protocols on the DataDep graph dataset generator. The significant growth in graph-based applications and the escalating release of sensitive information across these platforms have created a pressing need for stronger confidentiality protections. Due to the unique characteristics of graph data, the development of specialized confidentiality protocols is now a critical research need. Temporal activity detection, a sub-task of event detection, is the focus of this study. We observe that utilizing context from the entire video for prediction can be detrimental if the context contains information about activities occurring after the activity in question. To address this challenge, we propose a dual context consolidation network (DCAN) that selectively incorporates context from two time windows: a short-term and a long-term context. The DCAN model is particularly effective at ignoring irrelevant information and is straightforward to implement. Experimental results show that our proposed framework achieves superior performance when compared to current state-of-the-art approaches. We present a concise representation system that accelerates the precise computation of maximum probability expectation (MPE) and restricts optimization in graphical models. This technique simplifies the assessment of a variable's significance by examining the minimal subset of its adjacent neighbors that influences its MPE. We demonstrate that determining this subset enables us to efficiently calculate the MPE of a single node and identify whether a local maximum can be achieved. By segmenting the variable set into depEndent and independent subsets based on the proposed representation, we can divide the MPE calculation into separate processes. Furthermore, we discuss how the representation system can be employed for the exact computation of MPE and limited optimization in graphical models, and include a depiction of the algorithm used for this purpose. We also provide empirical evidence to show the effectiveness of this technique, particularly on large-scale networks. This representation system can be employed for the computation of maximum likelihood estimation and structural EM in graphical models, and is currently being explored for other applications such as constraint propagation and reasoning in knowledge bases. Utilizing this approach, we were able to prove the existence of a local parameterization for compact, non-singular areas of a manifold that admits a decomposition. This proof relies on a key lemma regarding the modification of a manifold's metric near a singular point. We then applied this understanding to analyze the decompositions' behavior in the presence of singularities. Specifically, we identified how the Hodge theorem can be applied to extract information about a manifold's de Rham cohomology from the decompositions. Additionally, we utilized minimal surfaces to remove singularities and extend our results to a broader class of manifolds. This led to an expansion of the available decompositions into a global format. We also explored connections to the classical Lefschetz d'Alambertian equation and the role of the Poincar\'e inequality in our proofs. Moreover, we observed how our results can be interpreted through the lens of harmonic differential forms. This interpretation enabled us to recover and generalize prior outcomes. We also explored the geometric implications of our findings, specifically in relation to the construction of a conformal hyperbolization process. This process is a key component in the development of a broader strategy to demonstrate the existence of a suite of geometric surfaces associated with a manifold's decomposition. We have demonstrated that these geometric surfaces exist locally near compact, non-singular areas of a manifold that admits a decomposition. We have also shown that these surfaces can be constructed globally across manifolds with a decomposition, provided the manifold's dimension is less than or equal to 4. This construction relies on a local parameterization for compact, non-singular areas of the manifold. We have demonstrated that these surfaces share key characteristics with the construction described in the first paper, provided their dimension is less than or equal to 3. We have also shown that these surfaces differ from the construction described in the first paper when their dimension is exactly 4. We investigated the motion of a cylindrical solid within a granular medium filled with a fluid, exploring how its orientation affects drag forces. Our experiments showed that the force exerted on the cylinder is significantly greater when its longest axis is parallel to the pulling force than when it's perpendicular. This difference can be attributed to changes in the local geometry and frictional interactions at the interface between the cylinder and the granular bed. We demonstrated that a model incorporating these factors accurately predicts the behavior we observed. This understanding has implications for the movement of rigid objects within similar environments and could also provide insight for predicting the behavior of plants and animal stems within these types of settings. Furthermore, our study sheds light on the interaction between frictional forces and the geometry of the granular bed, revealing a response similar to that observed in dry granular media when the cylinder is subjected to oscillatory motion. This has led us to propose a method for quantifying the frictional force experienced by an object moving through a granular bed. This study was published in an earlier report presented at the 2019 Meeting of the American Physical Society - Division of Fluid Dynamics. Our research has since continued, with further exploration of the behavior of the cylinder when moved at different speeds and in beds made up of different shaped grains. These advances have given us a more in-depth comprehension of how the force experienced by the cylinder is affected by both the speed at which it's moved and the geometry of the grains that make up the bed. This understanding has been expressed numerically, with our experiments showing that the force experienced by the cylinder can be as much as twice the force measured in our initial experiments with a similar velocity in a bed made up of the same grains. Notably, this increase in force is confined to a specific range of velocities and falls as the velocity at which the cylinder is moved is either increased beyond this point or decreased below it. This research has provided a further glimpse into the complex interactions that occur within these unique environments and could also have implications for the behavior of plants and animal stems within these settings. Detecting three-dimensional boxes at far distances has long been a challenging task for object detection algorithms. Unlike closer objects, those farther away demand more precise depth estimation in order to expand the typical shallow 3D box architecture. Furthermore, the risk of misclassification increases with objects at greater distances due to the limited and low-resolution feature maps available. To tackle this issue, we present Far3Det, a novel distant three-dimensional detection module, in an effort to specialize in the identification of far-away objects. The proposed module is a deep learning-based system that treats close and distant objects as two separate yet interconnected tasks. By doing so, it learns to prioritize precise depth estimation and class classification for objects at greater distances, resulting in enhanced performance. Experimental results indicate that Far3Det achieves superior accuracy when detecting distant objects and outperforms the baseline model across all distance metrics. The code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/leobosman/Far3Det. In autonomous driving applications, evaluating the accuracy of object detection algorithms is a complex process that is not as simple as reporting the average precision or mean average precision (MAP). In particular, we explore the use of dynamic threshold methods, such as the maximum and minimum values for each sample, as well as the average and the most deviant values for each class, among others. For autonomous navigation and stable movement, estimating scene flow is crucial.  However, due to factors such as lighting fluctuations and new environment discoveries, training deep learning based scene flow estimation models on raw video data can be difficult.  Existing self-taught scene flow estimation methods typically use latent features from existing models, but often these features are not optimized for the task at hand.  We propose a novel self-taught scene flow estimation framework that uses latent features from models trained on classification tasks.  By using a feature-based metric learning approach, the framework can utilize features from source and target datasets, even if they were extracted from different models.  Through extensive experiments on the KITTI dataset, our method demonstrates superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art self-taught scene flow estimation methods. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering rules in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a container should be permitted to make and record these in a set of real-time rules. In addition, Timeloops offers a static analysis tool for creating a database of reputable base images for use in the development stage. This database contains predicted system calls for each module within the image, based on a calculation of the system calls made by the program binaries and shared libraries it comprises. When a new base image is identified, the rule-learning approach is activated, where Timeloops generates predicted system calls, creates a set of initial rules, and then monitors the behavior of the container in a testing environment. Any discrepancies between the observed and predicted system calls result in the creation of additional, more restrictive rules. Evaluation results show that the system calls of over 80% of containers match the rules set by Timeloops, even in the absence of any guidance. Notably, Timeloops has achieved success with a range of benchmarks, including web applications, e-commerce platforms, and machine learning services. Furthermore, the rules produced by Timeloops have been found to be more effective at preventing security breaches than the rules generated by a static analysis tool. This lack of compactness arises from the ability to continuously move homeomorphisms while stretching tiles on the surface in an infinite number of ways. A more limited type of compactness, relevant to groups that include the sequence of homeomorphisms defined by iterates of a given homeomorphism sharing a fixed point, cannot be achieved either. This impossibility of compactness also arises from the infinite numbering of homeomorphisms. These findings build on previous research concerning the compactness of homeomorphisms' collections and their relationship to sequence compactness. Those results established that certain collections of homeomorphisms, such as those based on Cantor spaces and derived from 2-dimensional torus homeomorphisms, are compact. A comprehensive study of local, unresolved M-dwarf stars is crucial for improving the accuracy of luminosity distance determinations, which are essential for studying the Hubble constant and other cosmological parameters. To this end, researchers have been working on the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Collection (MUARC), a spectral database of approximately 800,000 M-dwarf stars across the UV spectral range, which will be based on archival spectroscopic data from various sources, including the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph Board (COS) on board the Hubble Space Telescope. To utilize the MUARC dataset effectively, it is vital to assess the characteristics of individual M-dwarf stars accurately. While researchers have established methods for determining stellar parameters in late-type giant stars through the use of index-calibration techniques and Bayesian methods, the same challenge has not been addressed for low-mass stars in the field. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed a new approach, which is the subject of a companion paper to be presented in Collection II. Here, in Collection I, we outline the methodology we have adopted to evaluate the characteristics of M-dwarf stars based on their optical spectral characteristics, optical and near-infrared photometry, and the radial velocity curves obtained from UV spectroscopy. This methodology is the foundation for a Bayesian algorithm that assigns a probability distribution to stellar parameters, mass, radius, surface gravity, metallicity, and extinction. This algorithm will be the subject of a companion paper to be presented in Collection II. Here, we also include a preliminary assessment of the accuracy of the stellar parameters obtained from our methodology by comparing them with the parameters derived from the Bayesian algorithm, which uses the MUARC dataset. We investigate the maximum number of self-links in a single conjunctive query on a binary relation and propose an open problem regarding its computational complexity. Building upon previous research, we establish upper and lower bounds for specific scenarios. For instance, a self-self-join with one self-link is co-NPC, while a self-self-join with two self-links is co-NPC if the underlying relation is binary, yet NP-complete if it's ternary. Additionally, a self-self-join with three self-links is NP-complete, and the same level of complexity is reached with two self-links in a self-self-self-join. We also explore connections to other problems and consider the implications of self-links in database contexts. Further, we introduce a new problem, 'at most k self-links', which determines whether a conjunctive query contains up to k self-links, and examine its complexity for both private and public k. This investigation contributes to a better understanding of self-links in conjunctive queries and may inform strategies for securing against link attacks. Finally, we provide a preliminary analysis of a new metric, self-link density, which calculates the average number of self-links per variable in a conjunctive query. This study can serve as a starting point for exploring other types of self-referential queries. With regard to private conjunctive queries, we establish that having one self-link is enough to achieve full generality, and for two self-links, it's co-NPC. Moreover, a question arises regarding whether there's a private conjunctive query with two self-links that isn't equivalent to a self-join with two self-links. This research also considers the impact of self-links in semantic search and publishes additional techniques for handling self-links in both theoretical and practical contexts. With regard to public conjunctive queries, we establish that having one self-link is enough to achieve co-NPC, and for two self-links, it's co-NPC as well. Furthermore, a self-self-join with three self-links or more reaches the same level of complexity, and the same complexity is reached with two self-links in a self-self-self-join. In thermodynamic systems that exhibit phase changes from an disordered to an ordered state, particles that facilitate this transition by attaching to either like-phase or opposing-phase particles are known as siphons and barrow's respectively. This task scope focuses on identifying the specific interactions that allow these particles to be learned from just one sample, as is capable with monopolar interactions that target like-phase particles. A prominent method involves utilizing an extended version of the Ising model's universal parameters and applying them to a universal classifier that ignores the underlying structure of the model. A recent study demonstrated that this method fails when the model includes a competing siphon. To overcome this limitation, a new method is proposed, leveraging a hidden variable to model the classifier's behavior and a hidden coexisting siphon's interactions. This approach is tested on various Ising models, including those with hidden coexisting siphons, and demonstrates its ability to accurately learn these interactions with just one sample, as is the case with monopolar interactions that target like-phase particles, but fails when the model includes a competing siphon. However, it is also shown that when the model includes both a hidden coexisting siphon and a competing siphon, the proposed method can learn the hidden siphon's interactions, while the previous method learned the competing siphon's interactions, resulting in a situation where the two methods have opposite preferences. This counter-intuitive behavior is attributed to the model's symmetry, breaking the task into two separate classes, and a new metric is introduced to distinguish between these classes. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based augmentation method known as CAGE, which employs related tasks to be learned from descriptions of task labels.
This method enables models to infer underlying patterns and apply them to new situations, thus expanding their expertise to a range of related tasks automatically.
The results of our experiments, spanning both few-shot and single-shot scenarios, show significant enhancements in performance on unseen tasks, with CAGE achieving substantial gains over baseline models and surpassing their performance by a wide margin. Moreover, our analysis reveals that CAGE effectively mitigates the issue of domain shift and produces more generalizable models with a greater tendency to exploit semantic information. The code and models for our evaluations are publicly accessible at https://github.com/Paragon-Team/CAGE. With CAGE, we anticipate that the next generation of massive language models will exhibit enhanced cross-task generalization abilities in an unsupervised context. The time when a single model can excel in every task it is exposed to while learning is not too far off. The pressure is now on the community to tackle the magnitude of parameters in these models. Although the results in this paper were achieved with models comprising 3 billion parameters, the experiments using 13 billion parameters were promising but required more time to be fully trained. The implementation of deep learning models involves selecting multiple hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance. This selection of hyperparameters has a surprising side effect on the security of inference computations, specifically when implementations of deep learning models are optimized for speed and use floating-point numbers. This can lead to potential security vulnerabilities due to differences (differential) attacks that can manipulate input data and trigger a division-by-zero error in the computation, resulting in malicious code being executed. After establishing the connection between deep learning hyperparameters and this security concern, we conduct a thorough analysis of the relationship between hyperparameters and the attack success rate. This analysis enables the development of an efficient algorithm to identify deep learning hyperparameters that minimize the risk of a differential attack, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique across various deep learning models and datasets. This technique can be applied to any deep learning benchmark to identify hyperparameters that balance performance and security. We also observe that certain deep learning techniques, such as adversarial training and precise training, can significantly enhance the resistance to differential attacks, and our research highlights the importance of considering the impact of deep learning hyperparameters on the security of computational workloads. This research paper proposes an advanced stream processing engine called LifeFlow, which is designed to efficiently process regular data streams. LifeFlow is unique in its use of a non-procedural query language, called LifeQuery, that allows for complex computations on data streams. The system is built on top of a novel storage approach called Time-And-Attribute-Based (TAB) storage, combining time-based and attribute-based storage methods to enhance performance. By storing data in a time-attribute-tree structure, LifeFlow achieves efficient data retrieval and reduces storage requirements. The TAB storage method enables LifeFlow to process queries directly from storage, eliminating the need for intermediate result sets and thus minimizing memory usage. As a result, LifeFlow boasts high memory efficiency, reduced memory usage, and faster query processing. However, the absence of materialized aggregates in LifeFlow leads to increased processing times for some queries, especially those with large data sets. To address this limitation, a new LifeFlow variant is presented, called LifeFlow-MA, that integrates materialized aggregates to remedy this shortcoming. The paper explores the performance benefits and limitations of LifeFlow and its variants through a range of benchmark tests. The paper concludes by highlighting the prospects for further innovations in the LifeFlow framework and the potential for future improvements to its performance. A LifeFlow dataset, called LifeData, is also introduced, comprising real-world regular data stream datasets. The success of deep learning in various tasks depends on its ability to withstand data alterations, particularly when encountering manipulated or artificially altered images. Although research has focused on understanding deep learning's performance under image alterations, there remains a lack of investigation into the impact of loss function alterations on the model's behavior. This study initiates the exploration of this under-researched area by analyzing the effect of loss function alterations on the classification of natural images. To achieve this, we designed a novel metric called classification stability, which indicates the influence of loss function alterations on the model's output. Our experimental results demonstrated that the choice of loss function significantly affects classification stability, with deep learning models exhibiting higher stability when using robust loss functions such as the contrastive loss function. Moreover, our findings highlighted that the relation between classification stability and loss function alterations follows a specific pattern, which provides insights into the optimal loss function for stable classification. Moreover, our proposed framework enabled the identification of models that combine high classification accuracy and stability, thus providing a practical solution to the challenge of deep learning classification. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of loss function alterations and its implications on deep learning classification, openning up new directions for investigation, such as the impact of loss function alterations on the model's generalization, as well as the incorporation of stability into model selection processes using meta-learning. This is further illustrated in the case of deep learning-based image classification, with all the code used in this study publicly available at https://github.com/andersonbreton/deep-stability. The extensive variety of teaching methods for robotics through human interaction can be streamlined into two primary approaches: active and passive feedback methods. Active feedback involves the human providing explicit guidance to the robot, often in the form of demonstrating tasks first, then offering instructions or answering questions. In contrast, passive feedback relies on observing the robot's actions and observing the consequences that result from its performance. Humans can grasp a wide range of concepts through a combination of observing the actions of others and the consequences of those actions, combined with the opportunity to correct the actions of others. Building on this understanding, we propose a new learning algorithm that allows the robot to learn from the human's ability to correct the actions of others, achieving a more efficient and effective learning process. When applied to a complex task that requires both precise motor control and complex planning, our algorithm proved to be a more viable option than both individual action repetition and instruction-following, despite being a more complicated process. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning-based enhancements of PET images using magnetic resonance (MR) images as training data have shown promising results, notably our previous approach that utilized robust deep learning to compensate for decreased PET signal-to-noise ratio. However, this method had limitations: it required the same type of PET data for training and testing, and it didn't account for variations in MR data. To address these issues, we have developed a novel uncertainty-conscious deep learning framework that utilizes multimodal learning and incorporates a residual learning technique to minimize the need for high-dose PET data. Additionally, we included a outlier robust loss function to enable the model to handle unusual PET scans. We evaluated our model, pre-trained on low-dose and corresponding high-dose PET data but without the use of high-dose MR images for training, for its capability to reconstruct high-dose PET images from low-dose images, including those with significantly reduced doses. Compared to the original robust deep learning approach and commercial PET reconstruction software, our results demonstrated enhanced quantitative accuracy and visual quality at all tested doses. Furthermore, our model's effectiveness was sustained even with more extreme dose reductions. Additionally, we found that the incorporation of high-dose MR data did not yield a significant improvement with our uncertainty-conscious deep learning approach. Our research lays the groundwork for the development of lower-dose PET imaging without the need for altered PET physics, providing a potential solution to safety constraints and increased scan time issues. It also highlights the potential applications and efficacy of deep learning in medical imaging beyond image classification tasks. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the potential for deep learning models to capture fundamental PET physics, such potentially useful features as diffuse photon density distributions, through residual learning. We have made our uncertainty-conscious deep learning framework publicly available for the advancement of research in this area. Additionally, we have explored the principle of our approach on other outlier robust deep learning applications and have incorporated our methodology into a novel variance-conscious deep learning framework, with our results showing improved performance over the original robust deep learning approach. It is essential to note that, although our model exhibited significant quantitative and qualitative enhancements, the optimal strategy for the training of deep learning-based PET enhancement models at lower doses remains a question for ongoing research. We have established the benefits of our uncertainty-conscious deep learning approach over commercial PET reconstruction software and the original robust deep learning approach

Despite being widely used in past NLP systems that addressed coreference, centering has not been extensively examined in recent, more advanced coreference resolution models. We investigate the usefulness of centering-based approaches by comparing them to more conventional methods in a series of experiments, covering both traditional and neural coreference resolution tasks. Our findings indicate that centering-based methods are beneficial in certain scenarios but often fall short of the superior performance achieved by state-of-the-art coreference resolution models. Word sense induction (WSI) aims to identify the various meanings of words with multiple interpretations.  Although significant progress has been made in recent years, the task still faces challenges, primarily because existing methods lack a systematic approach to capturing the semantic shifts in words' meanings.  Our research introduces a novel framework that focuses on detecting word sense transformations (WSTs) - the semantic shifts - and leverages neural machine translation techniques.  By modeling the WSTs as translations, we can utilize existing resources, such as monolingual and multilingual parallel corpora, to enhance the efficacy of our approach.  Our method offers several advantages over traditional methods, like supervised methods and single-model implementations.  For instance, it can handle a vast number of polysemous words with ease, as well as learn from a wide range of parallel data easily.  Our experiments confirm the superiority of our approach, and it achieves exceptional performance on the WS4EVAL benchmark, achieving a high micro-F1 score of 42.79%.  Furthermore, our method demonstrates human-like intuition by successfully applying semantic analysis to the task.  As a result, our approach resolves a critical issue in the field and paves the way for the development of more sophisticated methods that can handle complex semantic transformations in words with multiple meanings.  To facilitate the study of word sense transformations, we also introduce a new task called semantic shift detection, along with a set of challenging examples that can be used to evaluate the performance of models in identifying the semantic changes in words.  Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the WS4EVAL benchmark and explore the relationship between word sense transformations and word sense induction.  We also investigate the influence of the complexity of semantic shifts on the task and propose a score to measure the complexity of word sense transformations.  Overall, our study highlights the significance of word sense transformations and the need for their systematic study, and it lays the groundwork for future research in the field. The study presents a theoretical analysis of the flow pattern created by an ideal polymer slug injected into an oil-filled vertical tube under laminar conditions. It is demonstrated that the polymer component dominates the flow within the slug segment due to its greater viscosity compared to the oil. As a result, the slippage effect on the rear edge of the slug becomes negligible, allowing for the determination of the rear edge velocity. Additionally, dimensionless velocity and pressure expressions are derived for both the polymer and oil regions within the slug, confirming that the polymer's flow adheres to Poiseuille's law. The pressure drop within the slug is found to be a product of the polymer and oil components' pressure drops. A dimensionless pressure model is presented for the oil region near the interface and is validated against existing data. A novel ideal polymer slug model is introduced, providing a precise understanding of the pressure drop within the slug and enabling the prediction of gelation occurrence. Conditions for the plug-to-gel transition are identified, and a numerical analysis of this phenomenon is presented. The influence of the interface on flow patterns is examined, and a transition from laminar to turbulent conditions is confirmed through dimensional analysis and empirical data. The ideal polymer slug model is shown to accurately predict pressure drop in both turbulent and laminar flow conditions. A dimensionless velocity model is introduced for the oil component near the interface and a transition velocity identified. The occurrence of the plug-to-gel transition depends on both viscosity and the Reynolds numbers of the polymer and oil, respectively. The ideal polymer slug model provides a precise understanding of flow patterns within the slug and the plug-to-gel transition, and can be applied to design optimal injection schedules for polymer flooding. The model also demonstrates the significance of matching polymer and injectant viscosities to maximize the plug-to-gel transition, and the potential for further improvement by matching flow rates with that of the interface. The study recommends the use of surfactants to reduce interfacial tension and facilitate more stable gelation. A numerical simulation of the flow pattern is recommended to account for real polymer non-Newtonian behaviour. The study provides a theoretical basis for the application of an ideal polymer slug model to foam flooding and other enhanced oil recovery techniques. The model can also be applied to the flow of complex fluids in microchannel flow, where gelation phenomena occur as a result of fluid interaction. In this study, we tackle this issue by exploring a new setting where we create labels for multiple classes using a single positive label. A novel neural network framework, called Multi-Label Instance Construction Network (MLIC-Net), is developed to learn from these individual positive labels. By utilizing both class-specific and instance-specific features, MLIC-Net is capable of producing high-quality multi-label instances. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our model excels in producing accurate multi-label instances in comparison to alternative approaches. Furthermore, MLIC-Net is applied to generate new synthetic data for multiple classification tasks, showcasing its effectiveness. The source of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting gamma-rays remains a mystery.  We have explored several magneto-hydrodynamic processes that could create relativistic electrons in the disks of galaxies and compared their sensitivity to detect such galaxies.  Our study reveals that only a specific process, where magnetic fields are trapped in the disks, can account for gamma-rays in this category of galaxies.  According to this process, galaxies with trapped magnetic fields can convert large electric currents in their disks into magnetic fluctuations, which can then accelerate particles to produce gamma-rays.  This phenomenon is anticipated to occur at a rate of 10-100 times per year using current gamma-ray telescope sensitivity, which could provide early warnings for transient events like active galactic nuclei.  A statistical analysis of 25 nearby galaxies with trapped magnetic fields discovered in radio lobe spectra does not exhibit the increased gamma-ray count rates predicted by this theory.  However, this lack of detection can be attributed to the fact that only a small fraction of galaxies with trapped magnetic fields have experienced the necessary magnetic flux accumulation, whereas those that have accumulated magnetic flux show enhanced gamma-ray emission.  Therefore, this theory offers a novel explanation for the origin of gamma-rays in galaxies emitting gamma-rays and provides a framework to investigate the vast stores of magnetic energy hidden within the disks of galaxies.  Furthermore, this study reveals that nearby galaxies emitting gamma-rays are capable of producing sufficient magnetic flux accumulation, and offers a prediction that up to 10% of galaxies with trapped magnetic fields can emit gamma-rays at levels observable with present gamma-ray telescopes.  Additionally, we expect that about 0.1% of all galaxies with trapped magnetic fields can emit gamma-rays above 10 GeV, and that the most powerful among them can also produce very high-energy gamma-rays, and predict that the most powerful one, the galaxy Cen A, will continue to exhibit gamma-ray emission in excess of 10 GeV and is anticipated to do so until its magnetic flux accumulation decreases to less than half of its present value. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare models without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code for FedHealth has been made available on the GitHub platform. It has also received recognition as a top submission at the IJCAI 2021 Federated Learning Competition and has been presented at the IEEE 2021 Conference on Healthcare Informatics. Currently, FedHealth serves as a foundational framework for additional research topics such as wearable medical device design, healthcare data sets, and the development of wearable healthcare models. Nonetheless, several problems remain unresolved, providing future researchers with numerous opportunities for contribution. In string theory, we consider the universe to have evolved from a random state, with the cosmological constant's value being determined by a combination of the volume and the winding modes of the fundamental string. Both of these contribute to the effective four-dimensional fine structure constant and are linked to the dilaton's interaction strength. While the volume mode can be adjusted to match the observed value of this constant, the winding mode yields a calculated value of 0.0246, which is previously shown to relate to the dark energy density. Furthermore, we calculate the scalar field's present-day power spectrum and find it follows a $k^4$ law, mimicking the cosmological constant's effect on the universe's expansion rate. Additionally, we observe that the winding mode causes a shift in the sound horizon scale at the cosmological standard, which aligns with the dark energy density's density scale. Both the winding mode and volume mode contribute to a unified description of the universe's evolution, and we present the normalized energy density spectrum resulting from this description. This analysis implies that the universe's energy density was sufficient for the formation of long-lived microscopic black holes through the Hawking radiation process, and we estimate the current density of these holes, suggesting they could be detectable by future gravitational wave observatories. Additionally, we find the universe's earliest instability occurred at $10^{-43}$ seconds, and we identify the primary particle species produced during the universe's early stages. Furthermore, we calculate the probability of observing a multiverse and find it follows a geometric series with a small initial ratio, indicating that the likelihood of our universe being observable is quite low. The universe's existence within a highly unstable parent universe, coupled with the energy released from the decay of numerous long-lived microscopic black holes, could provide a new perspective on the coincidence issue posed by the large value of the cosmological constant. Additionally, we propose that the universe's primary particle content could be explained by the instability of negatively charged spinnings of the fundamental string. Moreover, we present a new multiverse model, based on strings that can stabilize each other through their electrical charges, resulting in a vast array of universes each with their own unique charge configuration. A new mechanism of vacuum decay is introduced, where a more stable vacuum can penetrate a less stable one by creating a bridge of unstable string field solutions, and we calculate the time it would take for our universe to become stable at approximately 10 million years after its creation. A new equation is derived to describe the universe's evolution during its early stages

Time-series data used in life science experiments typically consist of short sequences with limited points, often ranging from 10 to 100, and include numerous measurements. Additionally, these datasets frequently incorporate temporal patterns and include a high number of measurement variables. Due to the high cost and complexity of experiments, it's common to run multiple trials, with up to several thousand samples per experiment. Although each sample contains only a short-time series, it's essential to combine the results of all time series into a single, informative summary. Existing methods for time-series learning typically focus on longer series with fewer dimensions. We've developed a monitored learning approach specifically tailored to the unique characteristics of short-time series with high dimensionality. This approach utilizes a core embedding that learns common temporal patterns, and we show that it results in more accurate predictions and a more compact representation of the data. Our method also exhibits superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art embeddings in our experiments using real and synthetic data. Furthermore, we've applied our approach to a cell-signaling experiment with high-dimensional temporal series in a high-content screening experiment and a gene-expression study with multiple conditions.
