The accuracy of visual association detection models has seen significant improvement in recent years. Nonetheless, numerous applications rely on these models for daily object classification and retrieval tasks, and they typically suffer from a major issue: they are not able to handle incorrect positive instances effectively. We have observed that current evaluation metrics, such as recall-AP, fail to provide a clear indication of a model's ability to differentiate between genuine and false positive associations. To address this issue, we present a novel evaluation approach that assesses the performance of visual association detection models based on the density of incorrect positive instances in the retrieved rankings. To further enhance the robustness of the evaluation, we introduced a new method that incorporates diverse sampling techniques and integrates unique criteria for the negative pairs used in training. We have conducted extensive experiments on three prominent visual association detection datasets and have found that our proposed evaluation framework to be a reliable indicator of a model's ability to reduce erroneous positive instances. The evaluation results showed that the techniques we presented outperformed the baseline methods on every dataset and evaluation scenario. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures the benefits of parallel processing and allows for the execution of multiple concurrent operations. In line with traditional content-addressable memory functionality, our processor identifies a target memory location by mimicking the behavior of a search electron in a vacuum tube and generates an output based on the found memory content. By utilizing a combination of digital and analog components, we have successfully created a working prototype that outperforms existing implementations. Our design has been demonstrated to operate at a speed of around 5 million searches per second when built with a relatively basic FPGA. Furthermore, we believe our design has the potential to execute complex search functions, such as hash table lookups, at speeds close to those achieved with custom hardware. We have also explored the integration of our processor with a microprocessor via a memory bus and have obtained promising results. However, the implementation of a pointer update circuit has proven more challenging and further work is needed in this area. Diverse applications where our proposed Content Addressable Parallel Processor could be useful are also identified in this report. We have decided against disclosing our design choices through a patent application in order to expedite the development of our prototype and facilitate the learning process for academic researchers. With the advancement of FPGA technology, we anticipate our design to be a valuable teaching tool for teaching computer architecture and has already been of educational value to our research group. In the near future, we could consider the integration of a microcode control unit into our processor design. Additionally, we have considered the possibility of creating a simulated version of our processor using a software framework, such as Spike-2000. Furthermore, we have also considered the application of our processor to solve engineering problems, such as fluid dynamics and electrical network analysis, as well as its potential use in the development of artificial intelligence systems. We have been informed that our proposed processor design may be of interest to certain industrial companies and research institutions and have established initial contacts with a few of them. We have also considered the extension of our processor to include a memory management unit and a input/output interface, as well as the creation of a variant of our processor that utilizes a different type of memory, such as a content-addressable register file. A prominent court decision in the United States set a significant precedent when it ordered a defendant to decrypt an encrypted hard drive as part of an investigation. This decision has sparked intense debate about the limits of governmental authority to compel individuals to reveal encrypted information. Our work delves into the complexities of this issue, considering both the historical context of encryption policies and the underlying legal frameworks. We examine past court rulings, the evolution of encryption technologies, and the current state of affairs in both the United States and the European Union. Furthermore, we explore the broader implications of this debate for the relationship between authorities and individuals, particularly in regards to the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. Our discussion concludes with an analysis of the various arguments raised by scholars and the observations made by judges in previous cases. We also consider the differing viewpoints represented in amicus curiae briefs filed with the appellate courts. Ultimately, our exploration of this issue leads us to contend that the defendant's decision to encrypt the hard drive in question constitutes a fundamental exercise of personal autonomy and freedom. This perspective is supported by a straightforward application of established legal principles, including the Fifth Amendment's protection against self-incrimination and the Fourth Amendment's safeguard against unreasonable searches and seizures. Additionally, our work shows that compelling a person to reveal encrypted information raises substantial concerns about the Fifth Amendment's potential for self-incrimination, even if the encryption itself is voluntary. This concern is particularly pronounced when considering the various methods that authorities can employ to discover the decryption key, which may ultimately amount to an expansion of a search beyond what is constitutionally permissible. Our research also reveals that the government's position on this issue is built upon a series of misleading statements and a desperate attempt to undermine the very foundations of individual privacy. This attempt is particularly evident in the government's advocacy for the adoption of the "all-or-nothing" approach to encryption, which would render a user's data accessible to anyone with the decryption key. This viewpoint is contradicted by a comprehensive examination of the practical applications of encryption technologies, which demonstrates that this approach is neither technologically feasible nor accurate. Furthermore, our work shows that this "all-or-nothing" approach is an unmitigated danger to global data security, which would be inadvertently promoted by the government's position. The rapid dissemination of information on social media can lead to the swift spread of false news, which can then negatively impact opinion formation and political processes. While false news translation and detection have been effectively addressed through the use of neural network-based approaches in a single language, the development of methods that can handle multiple languages is an area that has seen limited investigation. Furthermore, the fact that news translation and detection often rely on large quantities of data related to each individual language makes it essential to explore methods that can learn from limited amounts of data. In this study, we develop a novel meta-learning framework, centered on contextual neural process networks, that is capable of detecting false news across multiple languages with only a small amount of data. This framework is then tested and validated through the detection of Spanish false news, utilizing both synthetic and real datasets. It has been observed that it achieves comparable performance to traditional methods that have access to extensive data, while also demonstrating a significant ability to adapt to the translation of false news into other languages. Furthermore, it is also demonstrated that this new framework outperforms the current state-of-the-art method for English false news detection, while also being highly efficient in terms of memory usage. Additionally, this study has a practical application aspect to it, as it has been incorporated into the FalseNewsAPI, a publicly available web API that can be utilized by anyone to only recently recognized counterfeit news articles. This API supports the detection of false news in not only Spanish but also Portuguese and English. All of the FalseNewsAPI's source code has been made available for public use through a GitHub repository. While false news detection is a complex task that is not fully comprehensively addressed through this study, it does provide significant contributions to the development of advanced false news detection methods. Furthermore, it also bridges the gap between translation and detection, while also overcoming some of the characterized multi-domain challenges. Additionally, it has also inspired a new research direction, centered on the development of context-aware multi-domain systems that are capable of adapting to new contexts, domains, and data formats. Finally, it has also been acknowledged that there are also certain limitations and potential risks that are associated with the development of false news detection methods, particularly due to the inherent bias that is present in large quantities of data, which are then utilized to train these models. Furthermore, it has also been recognized that there is a need for the development of more transparent and robust false news detection methods that are less dependent on translation, as well as methods that are capable of detecting false news that is based on facts

Our experiments show that the particles move more quickly near areas of high swimming speed and that their presence also changes the way the swimmer concentration gradient forms, resulting in a more gradual decline than would be expected otherwise. This effect, where the particles are drawn to areas of high swimming speed due to a similar preference for areas of high chemical concentration, leads to an interesting phenomenon where the particles become trapped in areas of high swimming speed if the gradient of swimming speed is strong, or move down the gradient if it is weak. This trapping or release of particles could be useful for controlling the distribution of microswimmers in multi-component fluids. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations of a simple model that includes an external flow, chemical diffusion, and the swimmers' activity and chemical interactions. Imitation learning is a strong foundation for training robots quickly, but it's vulnerable to errors caused by flawed demonstrations. This issue is magnified in imitation learning from small datasets, as existing methods struggle to compensate for deficiencies. To overcome this challenge, we're introducing close-to-ideal imitation learning with limited and inaccurate demonstrations. This task is complicated by various sources of error of varying severity and location. To address this, we're developing a statistical framework that assesses the quality of each demonstration independently. This framework enables us to differentiate between demonstrations that are inaccurate due to random fluctuations and those with systematic errors. Based on these insights, we're formulating the problem of reducing the disparity between the demonstrations and the target distribution. This involves creating a transformation that, while perfecting the data at hand, minimizes the discrepancy when applied to new situations. To solve this problem, we're introducing an algorithm that uses a transformation that perfects the data at hand and incorporates it with a latent variable model. This model enables us to learn the target distribution directly from the demonstrations. Although our algorithm ensures that the learned distribution will be topologically equivalent to the target, it may not guarantee perfect reproduction of the original demonstrations. This is because our method uses a transformation that while perfecting the data at hand may introduce errors in reverse. To account for these limitations, we're introducing an alternative algorithm that incorporates a constraint to promote demonstrations that are easy to reproduce. This algorithm trades off the goal of matching the target distribution for the goal of minimizing reproduction errors. This results in a model that while not as accurate as the previous algorithm can still outperform existing imitation learning algorithms even with abundant high-quality demonstrations. This is the first study to provide a rigorous analysis of close-to-ideal imitation learning from limited and inaccurate demonstrations. This research is an extension of our previous work on evaluating imitation learning algorithms. These findings are verified through comprehensive experiments on multiple latent variable models and datasets. This includes omniglot, minigo, and physics2d. Many learning methods rely on observation or demonstration, but these typically require expert input, which can be difficult to obtain for complex tasks. While previous research has shown that multiple agents can learn from each other using observation or demonstration, it's assumed that at least some agents have access to expert demonstrations. In this research, we explore a more challenging scenario where no agent has access to expert demonstrations and instead learn from each other. We develop a novel approach, called co-observation learning, which allows agents to share their experiences and adapt to each other's behavior. Our results demonstrate that this method can achieve similar performance to traditional observation learning when expert demonstrations are available, but it has the benefit of not relying on these demonstrations. Our approach is particularly useful in situations where the goal is to develop a range of policies that are different from what's shown in expert demonstrations. We apply this approach to a simulated robotic task and find that it can produce a variety of policies that are similar in some aspects but different in others. Notably, the policies it generates are often more robust than those produced using traditional observation learning methods. We also observe that the agents' ability to adapt to each other is influenced by the similarity between their initial policies, and that they are more likely to converge to a solution when these policies are less similar. We validate our approach on a natural language processing task and find that it can reduce the amount of data required for each agent to learn from scratch. Overall, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of co-observation learning in situations where no agent has access to expert demonstrations. We apply this approach to develop multiple policies for a robotic task by assuming that the agents are trained in different environments, and that the differences between these environments are reflected in the starting policies assigned to each agent. We demonstrate that this method can produce a variety of policies that are similar in some aspects but different in others, and that the agents' ability to adapt to each other is influenced by the similarity between their initial policies. Our approach is also suitable for situations where the data provided to each agent contains a small number of errors, and that the agents are more likely to converge to a solution when the errors in their data are less similar. In this work, we analyze parity-check accumulation codes (PAC codes) which are achieved by repeatedly applying a binary linear block code to the same data, with a varying number of accumulations. We discuss why the performance of PAC codes is best determined by calculating the probability distribution of the number of erroneous bits, rather than individual error rates. We establish a general formula for this distribution, depending on the characteristics of the underlying code and number of accumulations. We utilize this formula to derive two methods for estimating the performance of PAC codes, depending on whether the underlying code has a low error rate or not. We also present a simple technique for identifying the optimal number of accumulations in a PAC code, given a maximum error probability constraint, by examining all possible error patterns rather than relying on simulation. Finally, we apply these concepts to a real-world use case involving the transmission of images between spacecraft. We discuss recent advancements in the field, specifically the development of improved PAC codes and a more efficient decoding algorithm. We anticipate that our analysis will be useful for designing optimal PAC codes for various scenarios. We have publicly available a C++ implementation of our analysis and a newly created decoding algorithm. We would welcome any opportunities to further collaborate with the community on this topic.

Although it has numerous potential applications, the process has been hindered by a lack of labeled data. A major constraint is that annotating emotional speech requires significant time, effort, and resources. Our approach utilizes a continuous reinforcement learning algorithm to guide a primary classifier, allowing it to adapt to new domains with limited support. We test this technique on three publicly available datasets spanning multiple recording environments and demonstrate its efficacy compared to traditional domain adaptation methods. In particular, our results show that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to that of domain-specific training and significantly outperforms unsupervised domain adaptation in all evaluation metrics and recording environments. In our research, we address the challenge of a regularized decentralized learning problem in a graph environment, where the data sets are significantly imbalanced. Existing decentralized learning algorithms have achieved remarkable success in various applications by enabling multiple agents to collaboratively update their models. Nonetheless, they have encountered an important issue: the distributional disparity among the agents' datasets, which hinders the convergence of models. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new method, DR-DSGD, which incorporates a regularization term to mitigate the impact of statistical differences among the agents. Consequently, DR-DSGD facilitates resilient learning and converges at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{K})$ in terms of the final model's accuracy, where $K$ represents the number of communication rounds. Moreover, DR-DSGD achieves this resilient learning outcome while reducing the per-communication-step computation and information exchange, outperforming standard DSGD in both aspects. Thorough experiments endorse the efficacy of DR-DSGD in addressing the distributional disparity issue on various graph topologies. Moreover, our research is applicable to various loss functions, including cross-entropy loss, and the experiments involve natural language processing and computer vision tasks. The implementation of DR-DSGD is available at https://github.com/Parashar-V/dr-dsgd. Unsatisfactory models can be rectified with a single centralized update following the standard DSGD method. Additionally, we provide the convergence proof of DR-DSGD. Finally, our research demonstrates the potential to explore novel resilient decentralized learning frameworks, such as endpoint attacks and malicious graph topologies, thereby further advancing the field. Consequently, we utilized the JEWEL Monte Carlo simulator to examine nuclear modification factors ($I_{\rm AA}$) for jet hadron correlations at the LHC, considering three distinct jet energies (45, 60 and 90 GeV). Furthermore, we investigated how nuclear PDFs, thermal variations of the medium and jet energy influence $I_{\rm AA}$ across different quantities (charged hadron multiplicity, charged hadron $p_T$ and leading hadron $p_T$). Additionally, we explored the relationship between jet energy and nuclear modification effects. Our results indicated that the choice of nuclear PDFs has a notable impact on $I_{\rm AA}$, particularly for leading hadron $p_T$; moreover, thermal variations of the medium lead to an increase in $I_{\rm AA}$ by approximately 10%, which is $energy$-dependent. Lastly, we found that $I_{\rm AA}$ reaches a threshold at a charged hadron multiplicity of around 10 for 60 GeV jets, implying that jet hadron correlations contain valuable information on jet modifications throughout a medium. Our findings are comparable to those from the RENAMI collaborative analysis, albeit with some discrepancies. Nonetheless, our study highlights the significance of further experimental jet hadron correlation data, which would provide deeper insight into jet modification processes. Furthermore, we propose a suitable figure-of-merit for the normalisation of ratio data, thereby enabling a more precise interpretation of experimental data. This methodology may also be applicable to the interpretation of future jet data from the LHCT. Additionally, we highlighted that jet hadron correlations hold significant value in evaluating the properties of nuclear PDFs, particularly at low $x$, which could be explored in depth with anticipated electron-nuclear collisions at the LHCT. Lastly, our paper also examines the effect of scale, nuclear PDF and thermal variations on jet modification processes, which could offer a more comprehensive understanding of jet behavior within a medium. Furthermore, we investigate the variation of jet modification effects with scale, nuclear PDF and medium temperature, which could provide a more precise description of jet modification processes in various environments. Additionally, we discuss the significance of experimental jet hadron correlation data in evaluating the properties of nuclear PDFs

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scam operated through a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the scam's underlying structure, user behavior, and financial impacts. Our findings reveal the scam's intricate architecture, which enforces a complicated set of rules that enforces a form of hierarchical inequality among participants, with the code's self-similar patterns mimicking the golden ratio in their statistical distributions. Our analysis also shows the impact of participating in the scam on the financial stability of its users, with the likelihood of bankruptcy increasing by up to 10-fold after engaging with the scam. Furthermore, our study highlights the difficulty faced by participants in attempting to claim their invested funds due to the scam's design, with only a small percentage of participants able to escalate to higher levels of involvement, and only a minimal proportion of those being able to withdraw money from the scam. Our research incorporates both quantitative and qualitative methods, using transaction data, cryptographic methods, and even artificial intelligence, to achieve a deeper understanding of how pyramid scams operate and the risks they pose to users, especially in the decentralized finance ecosystem. Our study's findings have important implications for the development of safe and secure blockchain applications, as well as the creation of more effective strategies for detecting and preventing pyramid scams in the digital age. Our empirical analysis of a real-world pyramid scam also offers a valuable contribution to the body of research that aims to examine the underlying structures and behavioral impacts of pyramid scams in a data-driven manner. Our study's results can also be applied to identify potential scams, such as the one analyzed, by highlighting the unusual financial transactions and suspicious activity characteristic of these scams. Our analysis's use of multiple methods to analyze a real-world scenario, as well as our development of a scoring system to assess the severity of potential scams, can serve as a model for conducting empirical studies on scams and other complex social phenomena. Our study emphasizes the importance of incorporating the effects of light quarks, specifically the contribution of gluons, in calculating the differential cross section at various scales. We demonstrate the connection between the scale dependence of wave functions in QCD and the contributions of partons in the color singlet and admissible non-singlet states. We also utilize the Catani-Seymour frame to clearly identify the contributions from the light quarks and gluons in $p+p\to \gamma^*+X$ through the integration of the light quark and gluon phasespace in the MS scheme. Furthermore, we illustrate the relationship between the mass ratio of up and down quarks to the top quark mass in the context of the Drell-Yan process. Our results show that the ratio of up and down quark masses to the top quark mass can be determined with an accuracy of 0.0005 through the measurement of $\sigma(p+p\to \mu^+\mu^-+X)$ at a 100~fb$^{-1}$ data set with $10^9$ $\mu^+\mu^-$ events at an $pp$ center-of-mass energy of 100~TeV, or alternatively with an accuracy of 0.005 at a 1~fb$^{-1}$ data set with $10^8$ $\mu^+\mu^-$ events at an $pp$ center-of-mass energy of 14~TeV. Measuring the system's electromagnetic field relies on a two-step process: field detection and the measurement of the auxiliary system. We demonstrate the accuracy of this description by comparing measured expectations to those derived from a direct evaluation of the measurement process. This comparison considers different measures, such as photon number, coherent field state, and standard measures. Our analysis reveals that the measurement-based approach consistently yields the correct results, regardless of the measurement type. Notably, this includes the correct photon number measurement, which is commonly approximated as a projective measurement onto a number state. We show that this approximation is valid for coherent state measurements as well. We also examine the impact of system measurement on the auxiliary system and find that it results in the non-classical correlation of the system and auxiliary system. Finally, we highlight the necessity of a consistent description of system and auxiliary system during measurement, which we demonstrate using the example of measuring a coherent state superposition. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the design of experimental demonstrations of quantum phenomena with light-matter systems. Furthermore, we outline potential applications of our analysis, such as the evaluation of measurement-induced decoherence and the identification of situations in which the measurement-based approach may break down. We conclude by emphasizing the utility of tight-binding models in the study of light-matter interactions and the need for a consistent description of system and auxiliary system during measurement. We also suggest considering alternative measures, such as the coherent state, to fully comprehend the measurement-induced dynamics of light-matter systems. Lastly, we suggest that experimental demonstrations involving light-matter systems should prioritize accuracy over simplifications, such as the projection approximation, and that our analysis provides a foundation for the rigorous examination of quantum phenomena in these systems. The rising popularity of predictive process mining aims to use artificial intelligence to forecast future process behaviors based on historical data. Our research compares two deep-learning methods, LSTM and Graph Attention Network (GAN), for predicting business processes. Each technique has its own strengths and weaknesses, with LSTM performing consistently well, while GAN exhibited significant variability in accuracy across different processes. Additionally, the data normalization method employed by GAN led to unexpectedly high forecasting results on one process, underscoring the importance of thoroughly testing predictive process mining approaches. We advise practitioners to balance the potential gains from using advanced techniques like GAN with the risks of unpredictable performance. With the growing abundance of predictive process mining methods, further research is needed to establish best practices for applying these techniques in real-world scenarios. In the accompanying demonstration, we present an interactive interface for exploring and configuring predictive process mining solutions, highlighting the diverse range of techniques available and the variations in forecasting results that can result from different technical specifications. This is to showcase the variety of predictive process mining methods that can be tested and compared using the Raccoon Lake dataset, with each demonstration held at the CoDaPro workshop at the Conference on Business Process Management. The underlying dataset and demonstration code are based on the BPM 2019 challenge and have been expanded to include additional processes from the Raccoon Lake dataset, with further details available in the appendix. With the BPM community increasingly focusing on predictive process mining, we highlight the need for methodologies to evaluate and compare different techniques, as well as the development of more robust baselines that can facilitate reproducibility and productivity in research. Two potential methodologies for comparing predictive process mining methods are introduced, with further discussion on the advantages and limitations of each approach. Furthermore, the BPM repository has been established to provide an open framework for reproducing and extending research in predictive process mining, with the repository code and demonstration code now available on GitHub. A massive explosion occurred on April 12, 1985, on the surface of the nearby star AD Leo, emitting a huge amount of energy into the ultraviolet spectrum that was detected by the IUE satellite. By using a simulation to mimic the pre-eruption spectrum of AD Leo, researchers were able to study the extreme fireball that resulted from the explosion in the ultraviolet range. Although the eruption's impact on the star's behavior could not be determined due to a lack of continuous observations around the time of the eruption, the simulation showed that the fireball's emission lasted around 13 hours and consisted of a large amount of gas at extremely high temperatures, approximately 15 million Kelvin, which was however short-lived. The simulation also revealed that the gas's optical depth was so low that no significant amount of the eruption's energy could be absorbed, and as a result, the simulated spectrum in the ultraviolet range closely matched the observed data. Additionally, the simulation showed that the gas's curvature, or bending, caused the light that was emitted longest time to reach Earth last, resulting in a delay of about half an hour in the spectral lines' development. The simulation's findings were consistent with the star's behavior in the optical range, although the accuracy of those observations was limited due to the high scattering of light. The simulated data, when analyzed with a different technique, revealed an even more extensive amount of gas mass, a higher temperature, and a shorter time frame for the gas's existence. The accuracy of this technique, however, needed to be tested against more reliable measurements. The simulation's results provided a detailed understanding of the massive explosion on AD Leo and its effects on the surrounding interstellar medium. The simulation also offered a way to utilize the spectrum of a star's eruption to calculate the column density of the interstellar gas in front of that star. The simulation showed that this method was accurate, reliable, and could be applied to even more complex events, such as the star's mass ejection that resulted in the giant X-ray arc seen in front of the Milky Way. The simulation's findings were also consistent with more recent observations of the star and its surrounding environment. The star AD Leo is notable for having the closest known Earth to a massive explosion that could affect our planet. The eruption could have produced a large amount of extreme ultraviolet radiation that could have increased the risk of genetic mutations in humans and other life forms on Earth. The simulation's results showed that this radiation could have been significant, although it needed to be studied further

Three-dimensional point clouds are commonly utilized in navigation and safety applications, yet their accuracy is susceptible to fluctuations and outliers that can impede machine learning models. To address this challenge, a new technique called TPC has been developed, providing a robust smoothing method specifically designed for point clouds. By incorporating a model that identifies the orientation of planes within the point cloud, TPC leverages this information to suppress fluctuations and eliminate outliers through a separation process. This results in a smoothed point cloud representation that is then mapped back to a three-dimensional format. We demonstrate the efficacy of TPC by applying it to a monocular depth estimation model, leading to a significant reduction in RMSE error by 25% and a improvement in robustness to noise. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub. Moreover, TPC has the benefit of being efficient, lightweight, and straightforward to integrate into existing deep learning frameworks. In addition to enhancing the precision of point cloud representations, TPC also facilitates communication between computer vision experts and 3D graphics specialists by providing a unified representation of 3D data. This unified representation includes the geometric structure, and we envision future research opportunities to explore the incorporation of this representation into multi-task learning frameworks. In circular accelerators, beam losses and required reductions can result in prolonged downtime due to time-consuming and multifaceted recovery procedures. For example, recovering from beam losses caused by vacuum breakdowns may necessitate restarting the beam, waiting for the vacuum condition to improve, and ultimately resuming acceleration operations. In this case, beam reduction strategies, such as decreasing the beam energy or switching to a more stable beam profile, can be complex and time-consuming. Furthermore, modern accelerators often feature multiple beam lines and polarization capabilities, intensifying the difficulty of these procedures. Consequently, there is a growing need to explore alternative methods for managing beam losses and required reductions, particularly those that could streamline recovery procedures and minimize downtime. This talk will delve into beam reduction strategies, discussing various methods for minimizing losses and required reductions, and also cover case studies from circular accelerators such as the Large Hadron Collider and Brookhaven National Laboratory's RHIC. Additionally, this talk will discuss potential applications for new beam reduction techniques, like fast beam energy reductions, which could significantly minimize downtime and improve the overall performance of circular accelerators. Finally, this talk will also touch on the importance of collaboration between accelerator operators, experts, and software developers in implementing these strategies across different accelerators and machine conditions. This talk is an extension of an earlier presentation given at the 2019 Meeting of the American Physical Society, Division of Physics of Beams, and it includes additional context and more comprehensive information about beam losses and required reductions in circular accelerators. A perfect quantum annealing algorithm is theoretically possible, but in practice, it is compromised by various threats, including unwanted Hamiltonian terms and system decoherence. We investigated two scenarios in which quantum annealing fails: (1) when the Hamiltonian contains strong, anti-ferromagnetic interactions, as seen in some quantum magnets, (2) when the system is affected by environmental influences, as is common in solid-state implementations. Our studies demonstrate that structural changes can significantly improve the efficacy of quantum annealing, allowing for the anneal of non-stoquastic Hamiltonians and the mitigation of decoherence effects. The research focuses on quantum spin systems but is relevant to other applications of quantum annealing. We hope this work will stimulate further exploration of the interplay between quantum annealing efficiency and Hamiltonian properties. Our findings are based on numerical simulations of quantum annealing processes using the quantum circuit learning algorithm, with relevant Hamiltonians including the Kluver-Calsinger Hamiltonian and the Dimer Hamiltonian. We observed disastrous breaks in symmetry during the quantum annealing process when the Hamiltonian contained strong, anti-ferromagnetic interactions or was subject to environmental influences. These negative effects could be circumvented by evolving the anneal process in a time-reversal manner or adding a small amount of stoquastic perturbation, as we have demonstrated through our simulations. Additionally, we found that the optimal time-reversal duration is directly related to the relaxation time of the system, as we have shown through our simulations of quantum annealing using the quantum circuit learning algorithm. In the early 20th century, Johan Louis Emil Dreyer developed the New General Catalogue (NGC), a comprehensive list of notable astronomical objects that would become a cornerstone of celestial research. This list, finalized in 1888 but available in a recent revised edition from 1926, has significant influence on the development of modern astronomy. This thesis research delves into the history surrounding the creation of the NGC and its users from its inception to the early 20th century. A key focus is on Adriaan van Maanen, a former student of Johan Louis Emil Dreyer, and later Pieter Johannes van Rhijn in the Netherlands. Van Rhijn's work at Kapteyn's Astronomical Institute is also explored, particularly his use of the NGC and the development of the scheme of chosen areas to study stellar populations. This study is a significant expansion of previous research on the subject and is presented as a contribution to the history of the NGC and its impact on astronomical research. It is the outcome of research conducted in 2009-2010 at the Kapteyn Institute and is now made available in this thesis format. This paper introduces a novel framework called Regional Evaluator Training (RET), which adapts the successful evaluator network approach from efficient neural network training methods for use in model-parallel learning techniques. By limiting communication between model components, model parallelization speeds up training by leveraging multiple computing devices, but it increases the memory requirements and complicates the computation process. In contrast, the evaluator network approach facilitates parallel computation and reduces calculations, but it results in a slow convergence rate. The RET framework bridges this gap by introducing a new optimization objective that combines the data-driven evaluator loss and the evaluator-induced model loss. Our experimental results demonstrate that RET achieves comparable or better performance to traditional stochastic gradient descent and other parallel training methods for deep neural networks, despite using a significantly smaller batch size. Moreover, RET is more versatile, allowing the use of various loss functions and optimization algorithms, and it significantly reduces the memory requirements for deep neural networks with vast parameters. The RET framework can be applied to a broad range of model-parallel learning scenarios, including ring and tensor parallelization, and it has a simple and efficient implementation. We have made the RET framework publicly available through a open-source code release. In this work, we examine Euclidean space representations via geometric tensors and investigate various geometric quantities including volume, surface area, and Minkowski volume, analyzing their relationships and relevant properties. We demonstrate how these entities change under the action of affine transformations and determine their minimum and maximum values, also identifying the conditions for their equality. Additionally, we establish a connection between the geometric tensors and the moment tensors used in moment theory, showing that the used tensors are a specific version of the moment tensors. This connection enables us to apply established results from moment theory to the geometric tensors. Finally, we introduce an order-based classification for geometric tensors and identify the effects of transformations on the geometric tensors' order. This classification demonstrates the uniqueness of the Euclidean space geometric tensors within the broader class of geometric tensors. We conclude our study by exploring potential applications of geometric tensors in other contexts. This investigation seeks to provide insight into the impact of remote learning on students' ability to maintain pace with the curriculum during the pandemic. We believe that the effect of remote learning varies greatly depending on several key factors, including online platform experience, parental support, and technical difficulties. However, the literature lacks a comprehensive examination of these influential elements, which we aim to explore through a quantitative analysis of over 1 million course ratings from the online learning platform, Coursera, collected between 2017 and 2020. Our results reveal significant disparities in learning outcomes based on students' prior experience with online learning, with those who were familiar performing 12% better, and those who were less experienced with online learning performing 10% lower, in addition to the overall negative effects of increased parental responsibilities and limited access to digital technology. Moreover, we observe a 15% improvement in learning outcomes when these challenges are mitigated through better technical infrastructure and parental support. Furthermore, we find that the emergence of the pandemic led to a more pronounced decline in learning outcomes, resulting in a 10% greater effect, and also discovered a persistent pandemic-related effect of 5% in 2020, indicating that extra support should be continued in subsequent years. Our study offers a comprehensive examination of the effect of remote learning and provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to a broader context of educational research. We also examine the transmission of biautomatic properties in group extensions, including direct products, quotient groups, and group extensions by autonomous groups, resulting in several applicable theorems. Lastly, we conclude with several open questions related to biautomatic structures in group theory. Humans naturally walk with a varying gait, influenced by their natural stride frequency and ambulatory pattern. Understanding the underlying brain signals that generate these dynamic gait patterns can provide valuable insights for both healthy individuals and those with movement disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, for effective treatment and rehabilitation strategies. Current studies on brain-control of locomotion, utilizing invasive electrophysiological recordings from the spinal cord and peripheral nerves, have primarily focused on binary control of walking and standing. This existing research doesn't address the complex aspects of gait patterns, which are crucial for maintaining balance during ambulation. A novel approach is presented here, where the complex dynamics of gait are controlled through a neural prosthesis controlled by recordings from the electrocorticogram (ECoG) in humans. By analyzing ECoG signals during ambulation, our results demonstrate the ability to accurately identify different gait states and estimate stride frequencies, thus providing a foundation for the development of more sophisticated brain-controlled locomotion systems that mimic natural gait patterns. Although graphical models have proven useful for this purpose, their utility is limited by the difficulty of estimating a valid graph from data. We present an innovative approach to estimating a temporal graph that captures the non-stationary connections among time-series variables for their own forecasting. This approach is characterized by a temporal version of the Gaussian distribution, called the time-Varying Bivariate Distribution, and uses a deep learning method to estimate a temporal Gaussian Graphical Model. We call this model the Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity Estimation (DDECE) model, and evaluate its performance on real and artificial datasets. The model's code is available on the gy138 GitHub repository. We discovered that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods for time-series forecasting and clustering tasks. The DDECE model excels particularly in scenarios with changing patterns and variables that require flexible modeling. The code is now also on https://github.com/gy138/gy138.git. The deep learning technique we introduced has the potential to be applied to other statistical models, such as time-series variations of autoregressive models, and we are exploring this possibility in present and future research. The DDECE model represents a significant advancement in the field of time-series forecasting, and we are confident that it will contribute to the development of innovative algorithms for forecasting real-time data, such as streaming data and economic indicators, and will facilitate the use of historical time-series data in predictive modeling. The DDECE model is an important step towards the creation of a new generation of time-series forecasting algorithms that are capable of handling complex patterns, and we are exploring ways to make it even more effective, such as incorporating new optimization techniques, robust loss functions, and the use of biological and artificial neural networks. The DDECE model has the potential to be applied to a wide range of problems, such as the forecasting of energy consumption, financial transactions, climate indicators, and biomedical signals, and we are confident that it will continue to excel in the field of time-series forecasting. In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, achieving naturalness to resolve the hierarchy problem requires precise fine-tuning unless the stop mass is large. This study explores natural MSSM scenarios with complex stop interactions, focusing on the impact on the on-shell Higgs boson mass and its properties. The necessary fine-tuning is adequately represented by small values of $|X_t|$, with no significant dependence on the stop soft mass matrix's specific structure. The predicted on-shell Higgs mass falls within the 125 GeV - 126 GeV range, with $|X_t|$ accounting for the bulk of the contribution to $y_H$. The calculated top-Yukawa coupling, primarily influenced by $X_t$'s diagonal elements, can deviate from the SM value by as much as ±5%. The predicted top-quark pair production cross-section falls within the range of 0.6 to 0.7 times the SM value. The study extends to natural scenarios with heavy, non-degenerate third-generation squarks, with implications for stop and sbottom direct discovery limits, which could be as low as 3-4 TeV. The study also examines sbottom threshold effects on the neutral Higgs sector and predicts the sbottom direct discovery limit to be below 1 TeV. We assess the linearity assumption in network autoregressive models, which have gained popularity for their flexible representation of dynamic systems and ability to conduct structural change-in-variability analysis. By exploring alternative approaches to evaluate linearity, we analyze the performance of conventional and robust linear statistics in estimating linearity parameters. As a result, we introduce a novel nonlinear statistic tailored to network autoregressive models, which surpasses existing methods in accuracy. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach through numerical experiments and real-world applications, highlighting its potential for identifying latent nonlinear dynamics within complex network autoregressive systems. The proposed method is accompanied by an implemented R function for ease of use. Furthermore, we explore a new concept of linearity strength, which measures the magnitude of nonlinear effects, and provide a corresponding new R function to compute this metric. Our results show that linearity strength can vary substantially, often mirroring the findings of previous research on nonlinear dynamics. The minimal electrohydrodynamic system consists of a droplet with a charge, situated within a gas surrounded by conducting walls. When the temperature difference between the droplet and its surroundings is significant, a notable threat to droplet stability emerges from the onset of heat transfer mediated by convection. The convective flow that results can be controlled so that it appears as a persistent, three-dimensional fan shape. The formation of this shape is heavily dependent on the balance between convective and viscous forces, established by the Marangoni number. The droplet's spindles, formed during its transition from a spherical shape, serve as a starting point for the presentation of a theoretically derived formula that describes the shape of the droplet in both its spindle and fan phases. A discussion of the implications of these findings in relation to previous research is also presented. The range of the Marangoni number in which the fan shape is established has been determined through both numerical simulation and experimental observation. The results show that the critical point for the transition from the spindle to the fan shape can be as low as 1000 in certain situations, indicating that the droplet's stability may be more easily impacted by convective forces than previously thought. The emergence of the fan shape can be influenced by both increasing the depth of the enclosing chamber and reducing the amount of solvent within the droplet. The reason for this behavior is the broader spread of the solvent-saturated gas near the droplet's lower edge, which in turn results in a larger spindles-to-fan transition barrier. The discovery of the droplet electrohydrodynamic fan provides a means by which the spindle-to-fan transition can be studied. The impact of varying parameters such as the charge on the droplet, the temperature difference, and the properties of the surrounding gas on the shape of the fan can be investigated using this finding. A greater understanding of these phenomena may lead to the development of methods for controlling the spread of electrically charged liquids within confined spaces. Furthermore, the droplet electrohydrodynamic fan presents an intriguing mechanism by which heat can be efficiently transferred through the convective circulation of a confined droplet. This discovery may facilitate the design of novel heat transfer devices utilizing the transfer of heat within a droplet. A scheme for experimenting on the droplet electrohydrodynamic fan using an aerosol chamber has been outlined, and a preliminary report on experiments conducted with this setup has been presented. Although negation is a universal language element, its interpretation can be complex and dependent on explicit or implicit indicators. Current models perform well on tasks like text classification and sentence similarity assessment but struggle with more intricate tasks that involve a deeper comprehension of the text, such as CoQA. To evaluate the ability of models to comprehend text and reason about the meaning of words like 'no' and 'never', which indicate negation, a new dataset called CONDAQA is being introduced. This dataset includes 7989 question-answer pairs that models can use to assess their capacity to understand the meaning of words like 'no' and 'never' through a range of tasks like reasoning about implicit and explicit negation, negation based on the text's context and appearance, and whether a negation should be applied to a whole sentence or just a part of it. In complex information systems, entities and their relationships can be arranged in various hierarchical structures. Evaluating the validity of these hierarchies is crucial, though existing methods primarily focus on simplistic relationships, without considering the intricate connections present in multifaceted environments. This study introduces an original conceptual framework that can assess the inherent soundness of a hierarchy within an information system, regardless of the level of complexity. This framework is applicable to multiple contexts and can be applied by hand or with the aid of a dedicated algorithm. Furthermore, the framework supports the identification of implicit relationships that can enhance a hierarchy's efficacy. A concrete example is provided to illustrate its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. The proposed approach holds significance for professionals responsible for maintaining the ontological foundation of an information systems landscape. This is demonstrated through a case study on the expansion of a semantic hierarchy within an e-government platform. The focus is on the integration of novel healthcare services and the optimization of search results within an Australian government website, highlighting the challenges and solutions encountered. The expertise gained from this project can be applied to a broad spectrum of information systems and related fields, as illustrated through a discussion on the applicability and potential extensions of the proposed framework. The theoretical components of this study have also been formally normalized in a formal ontology to guarantee its robustness and precision. This has the added benefit of making the framework more accessible to experts in the field. The proposed approach has been successfully put to the test, as evidenced by the results obtained, and is now available for use in conjunction with a demonstration suite that is open to adoption by the research community. This suite can be employed to explore various aspects of the hierarchy calculation algorithm. Moreover, the dataset employed in this study has been incorporated into a benchmark suite that is also available for use. This suite comprises a diverse range of datasets, each representing a distinct application domain, and is the first comprehensive collection of benchmark datasets for an ontology-based information system. This study has a further contribution in the form of an innovative expandable model that can calculate optimal hierarchies in an efficient and effective manner. This model is the solution to an innovative algorithmic problem proposed in this study and is the first of its kind. It is an innovative expansion of the well-known submodular function minimization problem and is defined as the process of removing the fewest components from a comprehensive set to create a cohesive subset that represents the most substantial portion of the original collection. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium mixture of states as it adjusts the Hamiltonian, whereas quenching presents a sudden, isolated system following a Hamiltonian change. This study investigates the precise cover problem, where precise cover corresponds to the scenario where every element is adjacent to another, using the Ising model with competing interactions. Exact cover can be achieved when the driving rate is optimal and is subsequently maintained upon switching to a sudden quench. The research reveals that the precision of a exact cover is reached when the quantum annealing protocol is stopped, and the exact cover is still reached after a sudden quench. The study also finds that the fidelities of both quantum annealing and quenching converge to the probability of precise cover. The research further explores the precursors to exact cover during the quantum annealing process and classifies the regimes of quantum annealing and quenching dynamics. The results indicate that the quantum annealing interval can be recognized by the distinct peak in the probability of precise cover. The study also demonstrates that the critical Slonczewski switch can serve as an indicator for the precise cover by evaluating the precise cover after a quench with various switch positions. The research further shows that the probabilities of exact cover are equivalent for both quantum annealing and quenching when the critical switch is optimal. The study also finds that the probabilities of achieving the exact cover are better in a two-dimensional Ising model with competing interactions when compared to a one-dimensional model. The results also indicate that the critical switch becomes less precise as the driving rate decreases in a one-dimensional Ising model with competing interactions. The research further explores the effects of a one-step switch in a one-dimensional Ising model with competing interactions by increasing the driving rate. The study also finds that the probabilities of achieving the exact cover are better in a one-step switch in a one-dimensional Ising model with competing interactions when compared to a switch over several steps. The results also indicate that the critical switch becomes less precise as the driving rate decreases in a one-step switch in a one-dimensional Ising model with competing interactions. The study also demonstrates that the probabilities of achieving the exact cover are better in a one-step switch in a two-dimensional Ising model with competing interactions when compared to a switch over several steps. The distance between wave crests in the ocean, typically denoted as $2L$, is an important parameter that affects solar radiation absorbed by the sea, but its determination has faced challenges due to the lack of direct measurements. Although $2L$ can be estimated from the angular distribution of reflected solar radiation as observed by space-borne instruments such as IASI, previous studies have often assumed it equals the product of $L$ derived from wave slope statistics and an arbitrary constant, typically set to 1.75, for convenience. However, no thorough examination of this relationship has been conducted until now. Utilizing a comprehensive database of approximately 10,000 IASI scans over the global ocean, we have reevaluated this association under varying wind speeds and found the constant to be 1.85, with an associated uncertainty of 0.03. Notably, this value does not depend on wind speed, contradicting previous findings that relied on model simulations. Moreover, our research reveals that the accuracy of $2L$ estimates based on the angular distribution of reflected solar radiation is significantly higher than that of the cross-spectral method, and we provide a new, adjustable formula for $2L$ that can be utilized with optimal estimation techniques to retrieve more precise values of $2L$ from IASI data. We also found that both $2L$ and $L$ play a role in determining the angular distribution of reflected solar radiation, with $L$ exhibiting a greater influence, and we observed that the ratio of $L$ to $2L$ is generally greater than 0.5, with a slight decrease as wind speed increases. Additionally, we discovered that both $L$ and $2L$ play a part in regulating the intensity of solar radiation absorbed by the sea, with $2L$ exhibiting a greater impact at low wind speeds. Our research lays the groundwork for a full reevaluation of the relationship between $L$ and $2L$ and highlights the significance of accurately determining $2L$ in understanding various ocean processes and the ocean's interaction with the atmosphere. High-accuracy measurements of the gravitational constant (G) rely on the Newtonian definition of gravity and are typically determined through the drop method or lunar laser ranging. However, these methods are subject to significant uncertainties. An alternative approach involves utilizing the gravitational redshift of light emitted from the surface of a compact white dwarf star in binary systems. This approach is being considered for implementation in the Large Survey of ToO for the White dwarfs, which will include Gaia-like parallax measurements. While this approach is unaffected by systematic errors in Gaia's measurement of the angular diameter of the Sun, it is susceptible to variations in the gravitational potential along the line of sight, specifically the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$. Therefore, to minimize the uncertainty in G, it is necessary to constrain $\gamma$ before observing these binary systems. In the most extreme cases, a value of $\gamma$ equal to 1.001 yields the same redshift as a value of 1.000, requiring accurate measurement of the white dwarf star's parallax prior to observation. Therefore, this study examines the impact of $\gamma$ uncertainty on the determination of G using the drop method, lunar laser ranging, and the Gaia-like astrometry of white dwarf stars. While the drop method and lunar laser ranging are unaffected by variations in $\gamma$, the Gaia-like astrometry is subject to systematic errors related to the detection of the gravitational potential's effect on light as it travels along different radial directions. This study shows that the most significant source of this systematic error is the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$, which causes a shift in the determination of G that depends on the sine of the angle between the line of sight and the direction of the Earth's orbit around the Sun. As a result, this study recommends that the direction of the line of sight be chosen to minimize this systematic error, potentially reducing the associated uncertainty in G by a factor of five. Additionally, this study examines the trade-off between the accuracy of parallax measurements and the associated systematic errors, and provides an analytical expression for the optimal accuracy of parallax measurements in relation to the degree of contamination. Finally, this study considers the impact of the choice of the line of sight on the drop method and lunar laser ranging, and concludes that these methods are unaffected by variations in $\gamma$. Nonetheless, this study recommends that the drop method be carried out at a time when the Earth is located between the Sun and the drop tower to minimize any potential systematic errors related to $\gamma$. Although various techniques have been developed to secure ML model inputs, the focus has shifted to ensuring output protection. Our proposed framework, secure input-activation (SIA), combines the sensitivity of specific ML functions with mask-based code to prevent a malicious server from manipulating inputs and influencing the inference outcome. SIA employs a curated subset of activatable codes that are resistant to extension attacks. To optimize code selection, we developed an automated tool, simc 2.0, which identifies suitable codes for a given ML model and targets a specific input distribution. simc 2.0 outperforms the original simc tool and yields codes that are 5-8 times more compact while maintaining the same activation ratio. As a demonstration of its effectiveness, we applied simc 2.0 to enhance the security of several classification ML models against a hostile client. The proposed framework and the simc 2.0 tool have been made publicly available. This paper introduces a novel sorting network that distinguishes itself from
the standard sorting networks used in study of boolean circuits. Our unique
sorting network is comprised of a sequence of basic gate operations known as
comparators, where each comparator evaluates the relative magnitude of two input
values and yields the greater value as the output. In contrast to the standard
sorting networks employed in circuit analysis, where each stage consists of a
different comparator with a distinct binary input selected from a sequential
arrangement of input values, our sorting network employs a uniform comparator
stage in which each comparator operates on every possible pair of input values in
a random or systematic manner. We demonstrate that a sorting network with $d$
levels of depth $s$ and $n$ input values exists by analyzing the behavior of our
uniform comparator-based network when $s$ compares are performed at each stage,
yielding a sorting network with a depth of approximately $s\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ and
just over $n^2/4$ comparators in each stage. Furthermore, we observe that
this constructor-based approach results in circuit designs with a substantial
uniformity property, where every possible sub-circuit of a given size is an
elementary circuit. We believe this feature to be a beneficial property, yet
we fail to provide a formal justification for this assumption in this paper. It
is worth noting that the constructor-based approach to building boolean circuits,
like the construction of the sorting network described in this paper, holds an
appeal that is somewhat intangible and may be of use in other contexts.  We also introduce an alternative version of the constructor-based approach, where each stage comprises a single comparator with a fixed input selection, which we refer to as the sequential uniform sorting network. We then go on to prove that this variant of the sorting network is equivalent to the standard sorting networks used in the study of boolean circuits, albeit with a possible increase in the depth by a logarithmic factor. This equivalence between the sequential uniform sorting network and the standard sorting networks used in circuit analysis further highlights the novelty of our unique sorting network used in the study of boolean circuits.  We hope this paper will shed some light on the constructor-based approach to building boolean circuits and demonstrate the deceptively complex nature of simple boolean functions with multiple input values. We establish a comprehensive and consistent framework for consistent one-fluid objects in General Relativity, applying a sophisticated '1+1+1' relativistic hydrodynamics framework that differentiates between fluid components and the one-fluid approximation's effects. This framework is particularly relevant to describing binary neutron star mergers accurately. Using a perturbative approach for small differences between the two fluids, we derive a set of relativistic hydrodynamics equations that account for viscous interactions and surface tension. Our research focuses on the one-fluid approximation, seeking to identify the conditions under which it is valid and accurate. We develop a numerical method to determine the one-fluid interface, derived from the original two-fluid interface conditions. Consequently, we are able to apply the one-fluid approximation directly, without needing a separate interface evolution procedure. Our study reveals that the one-fluid approximation can result in an inaccurate interface width, leading to an artificial interface that broadens over time. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that for viscous dominant regimes, the one-fluid approximation can yield results comparable to the full two-fluid model, provided the regime's parameters are appropriately chosen. Conversely, for cases where the advection term dominates, the one-fluid approximation fails, resulting in an inaccurate interface shift. Ultimately, our study aims to provide a foundation for further exploration of the one-fluid regime in binary neutron star mergers, while also highlighting the significance of surface tension in these events. Despite its limitations, we anticipate that our research will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of binary neutron star mergers. In the process, we establish a new benchmark for numerical simulations of this type of phenomenon. Furthermore, our study raises important questions about the behavior of dense matter in neutron stars, which future observations will be capable of addressing with enhanced sensitivity. Consequently, our research will facilitate a more precise testing of matter models in future simulations of binary neutron star mergers. In the course of our study, we also identify a novel phenomenon associated with one-fluid objects in General Relativity, where the object's surface exhibits an unusual behavior due to the influence of gravitational forces, resulting in a mix of both fluid components at the surface. This phenomenon, which we term the 'one-fluid skin effect,' has significant implications for the behavior of binary neutron star mergers, particularly in regards to the production of heavy elements. As a result of our study, we anticipate that future simulations of binary neutron star mergers will need to account for both the one-fluid skin effect and the influence of surface tension in order to accurately model this type of phenomenon. Collisions between galaxies are likely to have shaped galaxy evolution, particularly those with sufficient mass to hold their gas within. This study explores how magnetic fields affect galaxy collisions, considering the impact on gas and stellar disks. Using high-resolution simulations, we analyzed three scenarios: in one, no magnetic field was present, in another a strong magnetic field affected the motion of gas and stars, and in the final scenario the field was weak and had little impact. The results showed that a strong magnetic field significantly affected the motion of gas during the collision, causing it to fall onto the central part of the galaxy instead of the outer regions. This led to more massive central bulges in the strong magnetic field scenario. The impact of the magnetic field on stellar disks was less pronounced, with a stronger field resulting in a thicker stellar disk. Additionally, the density of the stellar disk decreased due to the increased bulge mass. The final scenario with a weak magnetic field resulted in a bulge mass comparable to the zero-field scenario, while the shape of the stellar disk was a combination of the zero-field and strong-field scenarios. This study has implications for the use of radio polarization to study galaxy collisions, suggesting that a strong magnetic field can make radio polarization visible during these collisions. Further research on the effects of a strong magnetic field on the center of the galaxy collisions is warranted. This could provide a possible explanation for the presence of magnetic fields in galaxy collisions, observed through radio polarization, and may offer a new explanation for the formation of massive black holes at the center of galaxies. In the case of low-frequency, sentence-level grammatical errors, a significant challenge exists. Various models have been explored as potential solutions, but they often struggle with transfer learning and fall short in correction accuracy. Additionally, the issue of relying on the same source and target domains during training and testing needs to be addressed. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel approach called meta-learning for adaptive domain transfer, which allows a model to efficiently move from one domain to another. This method was applied to a pre-trained transformer-based architecture for sentence error correction. The results showed that meta-learning enables a model to effectively transfer knowledge across domains, outperforming non-adaptive methods by a significant margin. Furthermore, when tested on unseen test sets from the target domains, the model was able to adapt its parameters to a small extent, resulting in improved performance. This led to a reduction of 10% in the average error rate in the target domain and 5% in the test domain. The model's ability to adapt was validated through a user study, and the findings were used to explore the role of meta-learning in both domain transfer and generalization. The code and the meta-learning framework are publicly available at https://github.com/parag-ghoshal/fgerr-meta-learning. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of assuming a direct, certain connection between source and target domains. Instead, we establish a more realistic framework that acknowledges variations in both domains. The primary challenge in UDA is overcome by introducing a novel technique for concurrent, probabilistic mappings between source and target domains. This innovation enables us to extract a novel feature extractor that produces transferable representations for both domains. The proposed method is comprehensive, encompassing multiple scenarios, such as single-domain and cross-domain scenarios, as well as scenarios with distinct classification standards in the source and target domains. We validate our approach through comprehensive experiments on two benchmark datasets, showcasing its superiority over state-of-the-art methods. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/BDA. The theoretical analysis and the experimental results demonstrate the benefits of our approach in UDA. Additionally, we provide a novel explanation for the overfitting issue prevalent in deep learning through the lens of domain variation. This work has significant implications for the development of robust models in UDA and highlights the importance of accounting for domain ambiguity to prevent overfitting. This insight is further illustrated through an ablation study. We explore two practical applications of the proposed framework, obtaining promising results in (1) domain adjustment without label exchange and (2) domain adjustment with limited labeled data in the source domain. A study of 61 ultra-stable star-forming disks conducted by researchers has yielded a remarkable finding. Located about 680 million light-years from Earth in the constellation of Ursa Major, UGC 8839 exhibits outstanding stability properties in its gas distribution. Observations of UGC 8839 made with the VLA and SPW7 spectrum show minimal gas fluctuations, implying the absence of major gas episodes such as those associated with gas accretion and supernova feedback. Furthermore, analyzing the disk's composition using the MIGRATION2 code suggests that UGC 8839's stability lasted for about 10 billion years and may continue for another 7 billion years. Re-identifying the same individual across camera views in a surveillance network is a challenging task. Although recent advancements in facial recognition have improved the initial person-of-interest identification process, the re-identification of individuals in the wider surveillance network remains extensive and difficult. This study assumes that there are no additional references or a person-of-interest list and aims to efficiently re-identify a large number of individuals in the network, a problem dubbed as the "extensive re-identification" challenge. To achieve this, a new framework is proposed that utilizes contrastive training to learn a robust facial identity representation. The proposed framework is straightforward, (1) it extracts facial features from a neural network using a pre-trained model, (2) encodes each facial image as a vector representing the difference between that image and all other images of the same individual, (3) uses these difference vectors to train a robust facial identity representation through contrastive learning, and (4) utilizes this representation to match query images to individuals already in the database. The proposed framework is evaluated on real-world surveillance datasets and compared to other re-identification approaches. The results show that the proposed framework achieves superior re-identification accuracy at a very low memory footprint, a significant improvement in terms of memory requirements. The code for the proposed framework is publicly available on the Open Source Repository. This paper presents a novel framework for predicting extreme market fluctuations using a unique measurement method for tail risks. The proposed framework utilizes the achieved threshold measurement GARCH model, a development based on the previous work by Balli and Bleaney (2001), and incorporates an exponential GARCH component. A specific data set, consisting of daily Euro-USD exchange rate observations, is used to evaluate the effectiveness of this framework in forecasting tail risks. A simulation-based approach, comparing the performance of the proposed framework with alternative models, indicates that our model exhibits superior results in predicting extreme market fluctuations. Furthermore, a real-world application section demonstrates the applicability of this framework in monitoring financial tail risks for the Euro-USD exchange rate. Diverse prior distributions are investigated to establish the robustness of the model, and a notable finding indicates that the proposed framework outperforms the BGG model even when using diffuse priors. Additionally, this study explores the estimation challenges associated with the achieved threshold measurement GARCH model and highlights the benefits of utilizing posterior mode estimation. Bayes factors are also examined as an alternative estimation method, and the results show that the proposed framework performs better than the BGG model, and this advantage holds true for both the data sets used. The implementation of the proposed framework is possible due to the availability of the bgg and bggjb packages in the RYMA library, allowing for the estimation and evaluation of the achieved threshold measurement GARCH model. This twisted version was specifically considered for the flag variety $G/B$ and its Schubert classes. In our work, we extend the concept of twisted quantum $K$-theory to banner varieties, which are a more general type of varieties including flag varieties. This extension allows us to investigate the behavior of quantum $K$-classes in the context of banner varieties, and it yields relationships between the roots and coroots of a simple algebraic group $G$. Our findings also establish a connection between the quantum $K$-classes of Schubert varieties in $G/B$ and their images in twisted quantum $K$-theory, and we use this understanding to make computations of intersection numbers in projective space. These computations, in turn, provide a proof of the degenerate multiplication formula in quantum $K$-theory for the flag variety and its relation to the Fock space.
